exp.11:9:
This verse says that the Preacher sought to find pleasing words, that is, words well chosen and easy to receive. He also sought to write what was upright, that is, with honesty and accuracy, and that his words would be true. The phrase "upright" does not speak of decorating the message, but of saying things as they really are.

At the close of the book, someone speaks about the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth) and describes his work. Many believe the author is Solomon, though others think an editor added these final lines. It is emphasized that he taught with care and sought the truth, not merely to be pleasing. Then his words are compared to goads and nails: they prod and they hold firm.

For today: when you speak about your faith or counsel someone, aim to be kind, but never sacrifice the truth. Ask God for words that are clear, sincere, and full of grace.
exp.6:0:
It says that a good reputation is worth more than fine perfume, and that the day of death is better than the day of birth. "Fame" here means a good name, and "ointment" is a perfumed oil, very expensive in that time. The second line is difficult and is understood in several ways: perhaps it says that life can only be truly valued at its end, or that death teaches us to think seriously.

The book is attributed to the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. In this chapter he gathers sayings of wisdom, contrasting what seems pleasant with what truly shapes us. The verses that follow say that going to a funeral makes us reflect more than going to a feast.

Today we can ask ourselves what others will remember about us: caring for our honesty and our treatment of others is worth more than seeking renown or luxuries. It is also wise to reflect on how brief life is, so that we live it with wisdom.
exp.9:3:
It says that if a ruler or leader gets angry with you, you should not abandon your post or react with rage. "Spirit of the ruler" refers to his anger or mood. "Gentleness" is an old word meaning softness, calm, and meekness. That calm attitude can calm down great offenses.

The speaker is the Preacher, Qoheleth, who reflects on wisdom and folly. He has just spoken of the fool who loses control and shows himself for what he is. Here he advises the opposite: the wise person keeps composure before authority. Some understand "do not leave your place" as not quitting suddenly; others as not rebelling.

For today: if your boss or some authority figure becomes upset with you, breathe, respond calmly, and do not walk away or argue in the heat of the moment. A calm attitude can keep a problem from growing. As Proverbs 15:1 says, a soft answer turns away wrath.
exp.6:11:
It says that knowledge and money are like a shelter: they protect and give security against life's difficulties. But wisdom has a greater advantage: it gives life to those who have it. Here "knowledge" means understanding or learning.

The author is Qohelet, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just spoken of not longing for the past and of valuing knowledge together with an inheritance. Now he compares what protects from the outside with what sustains life from within. Interpreters differ on whether "life" refers to a full and long life or to something deeper.

For today: take care of your savings and your preparation, but do not depend on them alone. Ask God for wisdom to decide with humility, and let it guide how you use your money and your knowledge.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that the young man should enjoy his youth and let his heart be glad. The word for "young man" is one that means a youth, and the word for "youth" is the stage of life itself, both of which appear in the verse as "young man" and "youth." He walks according to what his heart desires and what his eyes see, but with a warning: God will bring him into judgment for everything he does. Joy is good, but it is not a life without accounts to give.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has said that life is brief and that dark days will come. For this reason he encourages enjoying the good things God gives, without forgetting that there is accountability before Him. Some understand the words about the heart and the eyes with a certain irony; others read them as a sincere permission.

Enjoy with gratitude the blessings of each stage of your life, but before deciding, ask yourself: "Would this please God?" In this way joy and a clear conscience walk together.
exp.7:7:
No human being has power over their own breath of life or can decide when they will die. There is no weapon that works in that battle. The word "power" here means strength or authority, and "spirit" is understood here as the breath of life, though some read it as the soul. And wickedness, the evil of those who practice it, does not save them.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally associated with Solomon, though not everyone agrees. He had been talking about kings, justice, and how uncertain the future is. Here he reminds us that death is a limit no one controls, not even the powerful.

For today: don't live as if you had your time assured. Today is a good day to make peace with someone, to do what is right, and to entrust your life to God, who does have control.
exp.1:17:
He says that the author came to hate, that is, to feel rejection and weariness toward everything he had labored for in this life ("under the sun" means in this world). The reason is that he will have to leave all that effort to another person who will come after him. "Hate" here does not speak of wicked hatred, but of deep frustration.

The Preacher speaks, whom many identify with Solomon, though the book does not say so with complete clarity. He is reflecting on death, which reaches the wise and the foolish alike. He grieves because no one knows whether his heir will look after or squander what he built with such toil.

For today: work diligently, but do not place all your hope or your identity in your work. Entrust your plans to God, serve with love, and trust that what truly matters is in his hands, not in what you leave behind.
exp.5:4:
It says that the child born dead (the "stillborn" of the previous verse) never saw the light of the sun and knew nothing of life, and yet this one has more rest than the rich man who lived many years without being able to enjoy what he had. "Rest" here means calm and quiet. The one referred to is the man who lived unsatisfied.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes examines life "under the sun." Earlier he showed that having riches, children and a long life is of no use if God does not give the ability to enjoy what is good (6:2). His comparison is harsh on purpose, to shake us awake, not to teach anything about those who were never born.

For today: do not confuse having much with living well. Be thankful for what God gives you today, serve with it, and enjoy it with gratitude, instead of always running after more.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that everything in life has its right moment. The word "season" means a suitable or fitting time. And "every purpose" refers to every human aim or matter: each thing we do or desire happens within a time that belongs to it.

Ecclesiastes is written by a voice called the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth). Tradition links it with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He reflects on the meaning of life under the heaven. The verses that follow show contrasts: being born and dying, planting and uprooting. Life has rhythms that we do not fully control.

For today: do not despair when something does not arrive or ends when you want it to. Ask God for wisdom to recognize what moment you are in: to wait, to act, to grieve, or to heal. Trust that He holds your times.
exp.0:8:
It says that what has already happened will happen again, and that what is done today has already been done before. For that reason it concludes that there is no new thing under the sun, that is, in the life of this world. The words "was" and "fill" in the older wording of the verse are rendered here simply as the ordinary forms the reader already sees above.

The one speaking is the Teacher of Ecclesiastes, who presents himself as a son of David, king in Jerusalem. Many identify him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He observes the cycles of nature and of human labor, and he feels their weariness. His purpose is to show that life without God, seen only "under the sun," ends up empty.

For today: when routine wearies you or you feel that everything keeps repeating, do not look for meaning only in novelty or achievement. Entrust your everyday life to God and do it with gratitude, because in Him the ordinary takes on purpose.
exp.8:13:
Here a very difficult situation is described: a small city, with few people living in it, is attacked by a powerful king. The phrase about him encircling it means that he surrounds it with his army, and the siege works are the ramparts and towers raised to attack it. It seems the city has no chance at all.

The speaker is the Preacher, traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He tells of something he observed that seemed to him a great lesson in wisdom. Earlier he spoke of how evil times arrive suddenly, and now he prepares the account that follows: a poor wise man saves the city.

For today: when you face a problem that seems much bigger than you, do not lose heart or despise simple wisdom. Ask God for direction and listen humbly to prudent people, even when they have no fame or resources.
exp.2:20:
This verse asks a question: who can be sure that the spirit of a person rises upward, while the spirit of an animal goes down to the earth? The author looks at death and sees that it is much the same for everyone: the breath runs out and the body returns to dust.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who reflects on life as it is lived under the sun, that is, from what can be seen. He does not deny life after death; he shows the limits of what humans can know. Some read the question as doubt, others as an invitation to trust God.

For today: do not cling to what you cannot control or understand. Give thanks for, and simply enjoy, the work, the food, and the people God gives you today, and leave in his hands what comes after.
exp.1:5:
He says he built large pools of water, to water a forest of young trees that were growing. The word that begins that sentence means "I made for myself" or "I built for myself." He did not only plant trees; he also made sure they had water to grow.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He is recounting everything he did in search of satisfaction: houses, gardens, riches, and pleasures. He wants to show that, even though he had everything, he found that without God these things do not fill the heart.

It is good to work, to build, and to enjoy what God gives us, but we should not expect it to give us complete peace. Today we can ask ourselves: where am I putting my effort in search of fulfillment? Let us put God first, and then enjoy the rest with gratitude.
exp.11:0:
It says we should remember God, our Creator, from our youth, before the difficult days of old age arrive. The verse of the old word for "Creator" and the word for "pleasure" are not needed here, since the reader sees "Creator" and "pleasure" in the verse itself. The passage speaks of years when a person will say: "I have no pleasure in them."

Ecclesiastes is written by a teacher called "the Preacher" (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. After reflecting on how fleeting life is, he counsels the young. The verses that follow describe, with poetic images, the weakening of the body: hands that tremble, a bent back, teeth that are missing, and eyesight that fades.

For today: do not put off your relationship with God. Set aside time each day to pray, read the Bible, and give thanks to him, without waiting until you have more calm or until you are older. What we sow today bears fruit throughout our whole life.
exp.7:16:
This verse says that the author observed all that God does and concluded that human beings cannot fully grasp what happens "under the sun," that is, in this life. However much someone labors to seek the verse, they do not find it. Even the wise person who claims to understand it cannot actually reach it. Here, the idea of reaching it means understanding or discovering it.

The one speaking is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has just recommended enjoying everyday life with gratitude, and speaking of people's tireless restlessness. Now he acknowledges that human wisdom has limits when faced with God's plans.

For today: when you do not understand why certain things happen, do not wear yourself out searching for every answer. Trust God, who does know, and enjoy with gratitude what He gives you today.
exp.2:17:
He says that the author thought God lets human beings go through tests so that they will realize something: that, when faced with death, they are not so different from the animals. The phrase "concerning" is the sense of "about" or "regarding." The word "manifest" can be understood here as "put to the test" or "show clearly."

The Preacher speaks, reflecting on life "under the sun." He has just seen that there is injustice even in the courts, and he takes comfort in thinking that God will judge. Then he points out that everyone, people and animals alike, breathes, dies, and returns to the dust. Some understand that he says this with irony, to humble human pride.

For today: remember that life is brief and that we are not its masters. Live with humility, do justice, and trust that God is the final Judge.
exp.9:9:
If the axe has become blunt, and no one sharpens its edge, then the worker must use more strength. But wisdom gives the advantage, because it knows how to prepare the work well. The Hebrew of this sentence is difficult, and some translations render it differently.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Ecclesiastes), traditionally identified with Solomon. In these verses he speaks of risky labors: digging a pit, tearing down a wall, cutting wood. His point is that practical wisdom helps prevent mistakes and wasted effort.

For today: before you push harder, check your tools. Pray, plan, learn, and ask for advice. Stopping to sharpen your method, your character, or your preparation can save you exhaustion and harm.
exp.1:20:
A person can work with wisdom, knowledge and honesty, and still have to leave everything they gained to someone who put no effort into it at all. The word for possessions is not used here; the verse simply refers to what a person has gained. The author calls this futility, something empty and temporary that brings no lasting profit. He calls it a great evil because it seems very unjust to him.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who is traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He examines life "under the sun," that is, from the perspective of what can be seen in this world. He is frustrated because he has no control over who will receive the fruit of his labor, and this takes away his hope.

For today: work diligently, but do not place all your hope in your achievements. Hold your possessions with open hands, and seek to invest also in what endures, such as faith, family and service to others.
exp.5:0:
He says that the author has observed an evil in the life of this world ("under the heaven"), and that it is very common among people. It is like an introduction: he is going to describe something painful he sees around him. The word "evil" here speaks of something that causes grief and imbalance, not necessarily moral wickedness.

The speaker is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on life "under the sun." Tradition associates him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. With this verse he opens an example: someone who receives riches and honor from God, but cannot enjoy them. He wants to show that having things does not guarantee enjoying life.

For today: possessions alone are not enough; we must learn to receive them with gratitude and enjoy them with wisdom. Today, thank God for something specific you have and take time to enjoy it with others.
exp.8:15:
It says that wisdom is worth more than strength. "Knowledge" here means wisdom or understanding, and "despised" means looked down on. Even though people look down on the poor wise man and do not listen to his words, what he knows still has more value than power.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, who reflects on life "under the sun." He has just told a short story: a powerful king besieges a small city, and a poor but wise man saves it with his intelligence, yet afterward no one remembers him. Some scholars see here a real account and others a parable; it is not known for certain. His point is that wisdom is valuable, even though the world does not always recognize it.

Today, value good advice without judging the status of the one who gives it. And if you contribute wisdom and no one thanks you for it, keep doing good; God does see.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that a person labors and works all his life, above all to eat and to sustain himself. Even so, his soul (his inner desire, his inner appetite) is never satisfied. The word "soul" is rendered here as it appears in the verse, and the reader can see the idea of an inner hunger that never gets full. It always wants more.

The Preacher (Qoheleth) speaks, examining life as it is lived under the sun. Shortly before, he spoke of someone who lives many years but does not enjoy what is good. He concludes that work, by itself, does not bring fullness. Tradition attributes the book to Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. His point is to show the emptiness of seeking final satisfaction in the things of this world.

Today we can work diligently, but without expecting money or achievements to fill the heart. Let us learn to be thankful for what we have and to seek in God the deeper satisfaction.
exp.5:2:
He says that a man could have a hundred children and live a great many years, yet if he never enjoys the good things of life and does not even receive a proper burial, a child stillborn is better off than he is. "Being filled with good" means being satisfied, truly enjoying what one has. Going without a burial was a great dishonor.

The one speaking is the Preacher, or Qohelet, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He is describing a common evil: people to whom God gives riches and honor, but not the ability to enjoy them. He uses an exaggerated comparison to show how bitter and empty that case is.

For today: having much or living a long time is not enough. Learn to give thanks and enjoy simply what God gives you today: food, family, rest. Receive it as a gift from him, not as a goal you never reach.
exp.0:11:
Here the author presents himself as "the Preacher" (in Hebrew, Qoheleth, someone who gathers people together and teaches them). He says he was king over Israel in Jerusalem. Where the original reads "fuí," he means "I was," and it is a way of speaking about his past experience.

Traditionally it has been thought that Solomon is the speaker, although the book does not give his name, and some scholars believe it may have been another wise person who speaks with the voice of a king. He presents himself this way to show that he had power, wealth and time to investigate life thoroughly. What he will say next comes from someone with experience, not from a mere curious observer.

For today: before you let yourself be led by any advice, ask where it comes from and what experience stands behind it. And be humble: even someone who has everything needs God's wisdom to understand the meaning of life.
exp.7:2:
It says not to leave the king's presence in a hurry, and not to stubbornly hold on to something bad, because he can do whatever he wishes. "Be not hasty" means do not rush. "Stand not" is the phrase that sets the thing aside: do not persist in it. "Whatsoever pleaseth him" means whatever he wants.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes gives advice about life. Here he advises how to act before a human authority, such as a king. It comes after a call to obey the royal command and the oath made before God. Some scholars think "going out of his sight" means abandoning service or leaving in anger; others think it means leaving one's duty lightly. The text does not settle this completely.

For today: when you are corrected or asked to do something hard, do not react with anger or walk out in a huff. Breathe, listen, and seek to respond with wisdom and respect, without clinging to what is wrong.
exp.6:8:
This verse advises us not to become angry quickly. "Be not hasty in thy spirit" means reacting right away, without thinking. The phrase "anger resteth in the bosom of fools" means that anger settles in and feels at home inside the fool. The fool keeps it and feeds it, and that is why he becomes angry easily.

The book is written by the Preacher, traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He reflects on life and wisdom. In the verses around it he speaks of oppression, patience, and pride. He says that the patient in spirit is better than the proud, and this verse continues that idea.

Today, when something bothers you, pause before you respond. Breathe, pray briefly, and think. That waiting helps you avoid saying or doing things you later regret.
exp.4:14:
It says that we all come into the world with nothing and leave the same way. Naked means without possessions, and returning just as he came means he goes back exactly as he arrived. Of all he worked for, he cannot carry away anything in his hand, that is, nothing for himself.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate the authorship. He has just described a man who saved up riches, lost them in bad business deals, and left his children with nothing. His point is that living only to accumulate is frustrating, like chasing the wind.

For today: work with diligence, but do not place your security in what you earn. Ask yourself whether you are using your possessions to bless your family, help others, and serve God, for that has lasting value.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that all the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea never gets full. The water returns to the place it came from, and then starts its journey again.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth in Hebrew. Tradition links him with Solomon, though some scholars debate who wrote the book. He uses the sun, the wind, and the rivers to show that life under the sun seems like a tiring repetition. He wants us to think about what meaning all of this has.

Today, when routine weighs on you and everything feels like it keeps repeating, remember that your worth does not depend on what you accomplish each day. Give your work to God, and enjoy with gratitude the simple things He gives you.
exp.4:13:
It says that riches gathered with so much effort are lost through "evil travail," that is, through a bad business deal, a misfortune, or a poor investment. So the rich man's son, whom he meant to leave everything to, is left with empty hands.

The one speaking is the Preacher, the author of Ecclesiastes, who is traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He observes life "under the sun" and shows that accumulating wealth brings no security or rest. The verses that follow say that no one takes anything with them when they die.

For today: work honestly and enjoy with gratitude what God gives you, but do not put your security in your possessions. Invest also in what lasts, such as faith, character, and love for your family.
exp.6:13:
When life brings good things, we should enjoy them with gratitude. And when hard days come, we should stop and think. "Consider" means to reflect. God allows both the good and the bad, one alongside the other, "over against the other" (that is, in contrast to each other), so that human beings cannot discover what lies ahead for them, or predict their future.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He reflects on the limits of human wisdom. He has just said that no one can straighten what God has made crooked. His aim is to teach us humility before what we do not control.

For today: give thanks for and enjoy the blessings of this day without clinging to them, and when a difficulty comes, do not despair or blame others right away. Stop, pray, and ask what God may teach you, trusting that the future is in his hands.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that God will examine everything we do, including what no one else sees. "Will bring into judgment" means that God will call every action to account, whether good or evil. Nothing stays hidden before Him.

The one speaking is the author of the book, called "the Preacher" (tradition usually links him to Solomon, though some scholars debate this). After reflecting on life and its toils, he closes his message with a conclusion: to fear God and obey Him. This judgment is the reason that conclusion matters so much.

For today: live with sincerity even when you are alone. Before deciding something in secret, ask yourself whether you would do it knowing that God sees it. And remember that He also sees the good that no one acknowledges, and that can encourage you.
exp.7:5:
It says that for every thing a person wishes to do there is a fitting moment and a right way to do it. "Judgment" here means the right way or the right time to give an account. But the burden or "toil" of the human being is heavy, for he lives weighed down by what he does not understand and cannot control.

The Preacher speaks, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on life under the sun. Earlier he spoke of respecting the king and of how the wise person recognizes that there are times and judgments. Later he admits that no one knows the future or controls the day of his death. Some understand "judgment" as God's justice, others as simple prudence.

For today: before deciding something important, do not rush. Ask God for wisdom to act at the right moment and in the right way, and entrust to Him what you cannot control, trusting that He does know the future.
exp.6:25:
It says there is a woman more bitter than death: her heart is like a net and a trap, and her hands like cords that bind. The "nets" and the "snares" were hunting traps. Whoever lives pleasing God will escape from her, but the one who lives in sin will be caught.

The speaker is the Preacher, traditionally Solomon. He is seeking wisdom and examining foolishness. Many understand that he is speaking of the seductive woman, as in Proverbs 7, or of folly personified. Others see it as a bitter experience of his own. The passage is difficult and is interpreted in several ways. He himself admits that he found few upright men.

Today: flee from what seduces you and enslaves you, whether a relationship, an addiction, or a temptation. Ask God for wisdom and make decisions early, before you become trapped.
exp.7:13:
This verse says there is something that seems absurd in life: sometimes the righteous are treated as if they were wicked, and the wicked are treated as if they were righteous. The word "vanity" means something empty, fleeting, or hard to understand. The author says that this apparent injustice is also vanity.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who is traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He observes life "under the sun" and admits that not everything can be explained. Even so, in the previous verse he states that he trusts that those who fear God will go well in the end.

Today, when you see injustice or it seems that faithfulness bears no fruit, do not grow bitter or stop trusting God. Keep doing good, enjoy with gratitude the simple things He gives you, and leave what you do not understand in His hands.
exp.7:4:
It says that whoever keeps the command will suffer no harm. Also, the heart of the wise knows how to recognize the right time and the right way, that is, the proper moment and the correct manner of acting. "Command" here refers to the king's order, and "judgment" can be understood as the proper way or justice.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He is speaking about how to conduct oneself before the authority of the king, whose power is great. Some think the "command" could also point to God's law; the text does not fully clarify this.

Today, when facing an authority or a difficult situation, do not act in haste or stubbornness. Ask for wisdom to know when to speak, when to wait, and how to act with respect, without giving up obedience to God above all.
exp.1:18:
Here the preacher asks who will receive everything he worked for. He does not know whether that person will be wise or foolish, yet that person will have power over all of it. The word for "have power over" in this verse means "to rule" or "to be master of" (so the verse uses "rule" and "master" in that sense). The phrase "I labored hard" means "I exerted myself greatly." He says this too is vanity, that is, something fleeting and without lasting value.

The Preacher, called Qoheleth, presents himself as a son of David, king in Jerusalem. Many connect him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has searched for meaning in work, wealth and wisdom, and it grieves him that everything ends up in the hands of another, with no control over what happens afterward.

Today we can work with diligence and with gratitude, but without placing our hope in what we will leave behind. It is wise to invest in things that endure: faith, a good example, generosity and love for family. As for the rest, let us entrust it to God with confidence.
exp.6:3:
This verse compares two places. The wise person keeps their mind on the house of mourning, that is, the place where people grieve for someone who has died. The fool, on the other hand, has their mind on the house of mirth, where there is fun and feasting. Fools are those who live without thinking about what truly matters.

The author presents himself as the Preacher, the one called Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He reflects on how brief and fragile life is. He says that at a funeral we are reminded that we will all die, and that this makes us think and change our course. He does not condemn joy, but rather the fleeing from reality.

For today: when you accompany someone in their sorrow, do not see it as a burden, but as an opportunity to learn. Ask yourself how you are living and what you should set right before God.
exp.2:10:
It says that God made everything beautiful in its time. He also placed a sense of eternity in the human heart, and yet no one can fully grasp what God does, from beginning to end. The verse has several possible readings, and the key word that some translations render as "eternity" is hard to pin down, so the sentence is open to more than one interpretation.

The speaker is the Preacher (Ecclesiastes), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. After speaking of the seasons of life (3:1-8), he reflects on the weariness of labor and the limits of our understanding. That is why he concludes it is good to enjoy what is good as a gift from God.

For today: you do not need to understand everything to trust God. Accept your limits, rest in the fact that He works with purpose, and enjoy with gratitude the simple things: your food, your work, and the people around you.
exp.0:0:
This verse introduces the book. "Preacher" comes from the Hebrew word Qohelet, which relates to someone who gathers or speaks before an assembly. He is called "the son of David, king in Jerusalem," and "Jerusalem" is an older spelling of Jerusalem.

The speaker is this Preacher, whom many understand to be Solomon, although the text does not name him, and some scholars think of another author or a writer who uses his voice. What follows is a reflection on the meaning of life "under the sun," that is, in this world, without looking beyond it.

For today: before accepting advice about life, it is wise to ask who is speaking and from where. Let us listen carefully to the wise, but seek to make God the center of our decisions.
exp.5:8:
It is better to enjoy what is right in front of your eyes than to chase after a desire that keeps wandering from place to place. What you see and have within reach is the sight of the eyes; the desire that passes is the longing that goes back and forth without ever settling down. The word "vanity" points to something fleeting, like vapor, and the phrase about vexation of spirit is like chasing after the wind.

The Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this, observes that a person works to eat and is never satisfied. Whether wise or foolish, rich or poor, restless striving leaves the soul empty.

For today: learn to give thanks and enjoy what God has already given you, such as your food, your family, and your peace, instead of living anxious about what you do not yet have. Being content does not mean stopping work; it means trusting God.
exp.10:7:
It says that a person may live many years and rejoice in all of them, but that he must not forget that the days of darkness will also come, meaning times of sorrow, old age, and death, and that they will be many. When he remembers everything he has lived, he will conclude that it was all vanity, something fleeting, like a breath. The word "but" in the verse introduces the contrast, and "young man" refers to someone in the prime of youth.

The Preacher speaks, who in this book reflects on life under the sun. Earlier he encouraged people to sow diligently and to enjoy the light. Here he balances the picture: joy is a gift, but life is brief and we do not control the future. Some understand "vanity" as emptiness; others, as something fleeting.

For today: enjoy with gratitude what God gives you, but live with wisdom, without clinging to what passes away, remembering that one day we will give account to God.
exp.1:0:
Here the writer speaks to himself: "I will test you with joy; enjoy what is good." The word "test" means to put to the test, and "good things" refers to pleasant things, pleasures. But right away he concludes that this too was "vanity," that is, something fleeting and empty, like a vapor that cannot be caught.

The speaker is "the Preacher" (Qoheleth), who is traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. After searching for meaning in wisdom, he now experiments with pleasure to see whether there is what gives fullness to life. His conclusion is that pleasure, by itself, is not enough.

For today: enjoy with gratitude the good gifts of God, such as food, laughter, and rest, but do not expect them to fill your soul. Seek God first, who is the one who gives meaning to everything else.
exp.9:7:
It says that whoever digs a pit to trap others may fall into it, and that whoever tears down a wall or fence risks being bitten by a serpent. Breaking through a wall means making an opening or gap, and a fence is a barrier of stones or a wall. Snakes often hid in such walls.

The Preacher (Ecclesiastes) speaks here, observing realistically how life works "under the sun." Earlier he spoke of an upside-down world where foolishness is in charge. Here, and in the verses that follow, he shows that every action carries risks, and that wisdom helps to prevent them. Some see in this a warning against wickedness; others see only advice about being careful in one's work.

For today: before you act, think about the consequences. Do not cheat or harm others, and when you have to "break down a wall," such as changing something established, do it with prudence and wisdom.
exp.0:5:
This verse describes the wind that goes toward the south, then turns around toward the north, and keeps circling without stopping, always returning to the same routes.

The one speaking is the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He observes nature: the earth, the sun, the wind and the rivers repeat their cycles. With this he prepares his complaint that, under the sun, everything seems weary and repetitive, and that human effort alone cannot change the cycle.

For today: when your routine wears you down and you feel that everything repeats itself, do not look to it for the ultimate meaning of your life. Offer each day to God, and find in Him the purpose that repetition cannot give you.
exp.6:28:
This verse says that God created human beings upright, meaning just, sincere, and free of wickedness. But people went down another path: they "sought out many inventions," which speaks of many schemes, plans, and clever devices. Some understand this as elaborate schemes or tangled reasoning used to justify themselves.

The Preacher speaks here, a figure often identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has just described how he searched for wisdom with great effort and found few people who were truly upright. Here he concludes that the problem does not come from the Creator but from us.

For today: when you catch yourself justifying a mistake with many explanations, stop and be honest with God. He did not make us complicated; he invites us back to a simple, honest, and upright life, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.5:1:
This verse speaks of a man to whom God gave riches, goods, and honor. He has everything his heart desires, but God does not allow him to enjoy it, and in the end others, strangers, enjoy it instead.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qohelet in Hebrew. Tradition connects him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He observes life under the sun and points out a common injustice: having much does not guarantee that a person can enjoy it. His purpose is to show that life is not sustained by possessions alone.

For today: do not wait until you have everything before you give thanks. Enjoy with gratitude what God gives you today, such as food, family, and rest, and share generously, because true satisfaction comes from God.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that two people who travel together help each other when one falls. The phrase "will lift up his companion" means he helps him to his feet. "Woe to the one who is alone!" is an exclamation of pity for the person who is by himself, because if he falls, no one comes to his aid. "Second" means another person who is with him.

The book is traditionally attributed to "the Preacher" (Qohelet), whom many associate with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. Just before this, it speaks of a man who is alone, who works without rest and has no one with whom to share what he earns. It calls this "vanity," that is, something empty. Here it shows the opposite: companionship gives value to effort and offers protection in difficult moments.

For today: do not isolate yourself when you go through a fall, whether in health, money, or spirit. Look for a friend, a family member, or your church, and also stay alert to lift up the one who stumbles beside you.
exp.0:9:
This verse asks whether there is anything of which we can say, "Look, this is really new!" The answer is no, because it already existed in the ages before us.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who presents himself as king in Jerusalem; many identify him with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He observes life "under the sun," that is, from a human perspective, and sees cycles that repeat. He does not say that there are no inventions, but that human life and the human heart follow the same patterns, and that this grows tiring if we look for meaning in this world alone.

Today, you do not have to rush after every novelty to feel full. You can rest in God, who gives meaning to everyday life and does not change.
exp.4:18:
When God gives a person riches and possessions, He also gives the ability to eat them, to receive one's share, and to enjoy the fruit of one's labor. That is a gift from God.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. After showing the emptiness of living only to accumulate, he concludes that the good thing is to receive the simple things of each day with gratitude. By contrast, the previous verse describes someone who lives bitter and without joy.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are enjoying with gratitude what God has already given us: food, rest, family, the fruit of our work. Today, pause during a meal or a rest, thank God, and enjoy it without haste or guilt.
exp.4:0:
When you enter the place where God is worshiped, be careful: walk with respect and attention. It is better to draw near to listen than to offer sacrifices the way fools do, who do evil without realizing it. The word for haste means rush, and the word for speaking out loud means speaking aloud.

The Preacher, called Qohelet, speaks here. Tradition associates him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He writes reflecting on life. Here he warns against a religion of empty rituals and rushed words, without a heart attentive to God.

For today: before you pray or go to church, pause briefly in silence. Ask God to help you hear his Word first, and then speak sincerely, with few words and without rushing.
exp.10:2:
When the clouds are full of rain, they pour it out upon the earth, and that rain falls without any way to stop it. It also says that if a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, it stays in the place where it fell. These are facts of nature that no one can change.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who according to tradition is Solomon, although some scholars question this. Here he teaches that there are things that happen by laws we do not control. For this reason, in the verses around it, he encourages us to be generous and to work without waiting for perfect conditions, because we do not know what will come.

For today: do not stay frozen waiting to have everything clear or under control. Do good, share, and work with confidence, and leave in God's hands what you cannot know or change.
exp.3:4:
The fool, that is, the senseless person who does not want to exert himself, folds his arms and does not work. "Folding the hands" means staying still, doing nothing. And "eating his own flesh" is understood in several ways: that he destroys himself, or that he ends in ruin because of his laziness. Some think it can also mean that he is consumed by bitterness.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally associated with Solomon, although this is debated. He has just said that excellent work arouses envy. Now he shows the other extreme: the one who does nothing also comes to ruin. The next verse proposes a middle path: better a little with rest than much with toil.

Today we can avoid two extremes: working without rest out of envy or competition, and the laziness that harms us. Let us seek honest work, with peace, trusting in God.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the sun rises and then goes down, and that it hurries back to the place where it rose again. "Hasteth" is an older way of saying "hurries," and the phrase "hurries back" suggests constant effort, almost as if the sun runs without rest to repeat its path.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. After asking what profit there is in so much toil, he uses nature as an example: the sun, the wind, and the rivers move in cycles that seem never to reach any new goal.

For today: if your life feels repetitive, do not measure it only by what you accomplish each day. Give your routines to God, and seek in Him the meaning and peace that simply going and coming cannot give you.
exp.3:6:
Here the author says that he turned again to look at life with attention, and once more he saw vanity under the sun. Vanity does not mean pride, but something fleeting, like a vapor, that vanishes and leaves nothing firm behind. Under the sun simply means in this earthly life.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth in Hebrew. Tradition associates him with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He has just spoken about envy and laziness, and now he introduces a new example: a lonely man who works without stopping, without knowing for whom or for what purpose.

For today: check whether your effort has a healthy purpose. Work is good, but not at the cost of your relationships or your rest. Set aside time for the people you love and share your burden with others.
exp.2:3:
The passage says that life has different and opposite moments: there is a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. "Lament" is an old word meaning to sing or voice grief for someone who has died or for a loss. It is pain expressed out loud.

The speaker is "the Preacher," traditionally linked with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. This poem of times (3:1-8) shows that life has seasons we do not fully control. The verses around it mix birth and death, planting and uprooting, embracing and refraining from embracing, as a reminder that life is varied and limited.

For today: do not panic or feel guilty for weeping when it is time to weep, nor for rejoicing when joy arrives. Walk gently with someone who suffers and celebrate with someone who rejoices. God can be with you in both moments.
exp.1:22:
This verse says that the life of someone who toils without rest is full of sorrows and burdens. "Sorrows" are sufferings, and "burdens" are heavy loads. Even at night, his heart, that is, his mind, cannot rest because of his worries. That is why the author concludes: "This is also vanity," in other words, something fleeting and empty.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He reflects on the frustration of working hard and then leaving everything to someone who did not labor for it. Afterward, in the verses that follow, he suggests enjoying with gratitude what God gives.

For today: if your work takes away your sleep and your peace, set a limit. Rest, be thankful for what you have, and hand your worries over to God.
exp.8:11:
It says that no one knows when a difficult moment will come to them. Just as fish are caught in a net or birds are trapped in a snare, people can be overtaken by a sudden misfortune. The words of the verse about fish in an evil net and birds caught in the snare express this picture, and the evil time is a season of calamity that falls suddenly upon them.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who is traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He observes life under the sun and notices that strength, wisdom, and talent do not guarantee success. Unforeseen events come to everyone, and for that reason he urges us to live meaningfully while there is still time.

Today we can live with humility and gratitude, without taking tomorrow for granted. That means doing what is good today: forgiving, loving our family, serving others, and trusting God, who knows our times even though we do not.
exp.9:6:
This verse says the author saw something reversed: servants riding on horses, which was a sign of honor and power, and princes walking on foot as if they were servants. In that time, riding a horse was something for important people. "Servants" here means slaves or attendants.

The one speaking is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He observes the injustices of life under the sun. Here he describes a failure of government: when those in charge place fools in high positions, the order is turned upside down and worthy people are left below. The verses that follow warn that rashness brings consequences.

For today: do not let yourself be dazzled only by positions or appearances. Value character and wisdom, and if you have authority, choose and promote others with justice and prudence.
exp.9:1:
This verse compares the wise person and the fool with a simple image: the wise person's heart is at his right hand, and the fool's at his left. "Heart" here means the mind, the decisions, and the desires. In ancient times, the right hand usually symbolized what is upright, favorable, and firm, and the left the opposite. The wise person leans toward what is right; the fool, toward what is crooked.

The author is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has just spoken of how a little folly can ruin a good reputation, like dead flies in perfume. Next he will say that the fool gives himself away simply by how he walks.

For today: before deciding, ask yourself which way your heart is leaning. Ask God for direction and listen to good counsel so that your daily decisions are upright.
exp.1:13:
It says that the wise person sees clearly where they are going, as one who has their eyes open, while the fool walks in the dark, blind to the way. But the author admits something that troubles him: the same end comes to both. "Event" means what happens to them, and "will happen" means it will come about. Here it refers to death.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who is traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He examines life "under the sun" and admits that wisdom is better than foolishness, but it grieves him that death seems to erase that difference.

For today: value wisdom, but do not place your final hope in it. Live with your eyes open, with humility, and remember that only God gives meaning and lasting value to what we do.
exp.6:9:
It says we should not ask with complaint: "Why were the former days better than these?" According to the text, that question does not come from wisdom. The word "cause" means reason or motive, and the phrase "were better" expresses the idea that earlier times were superior.

The book is presented in the voice of a Preacher or Teacher, traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate the authorship. Here the speaker reflects on how to live with good sense in a difficult world. Earlier he speaks of patience and of not being quick to anger, and then he praises wisdom. Always looking back at the past with longing can feed anger and dissatisfaction.

Today we can remember with gratitude the good we have known, but without getting trapped in comparison. Ask God for wisdom to see what you can do, with faith and patience, in the time you have been given to live.
exp.2:15:
He says the author observed something painful: exactly in the places where there should be judgment and justice, that is, in the courts and in government, he found wickedness and injustice. "Ungodliness" and "iniquity" are old words for wickedness and for doing what is crooked.

The Preacher of Ecclesiastes speaks, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He looks at life "under the sun," that is, from what can be seen in this world. He has just spoken about God ordaining the times, and now he acknowledges that human injustice seems to contradict this. But right after, he says that God will judge the righteous and the wicked.

For today: when you see injustice, do not lose hope or grow used to it. Trust that God will judge, and in the meantime, act with honesty and justice wherever you are.
exp.6:5:
Says that the laughter of the fool sounds like thorns burning under a pot: it makes a lot of noise and crackles, but it lasts only a short time and accomplishes nothing. "Fool" here is the person who lives without thinking about God or the consequences. "Vanity" means something fleeting, like a breath, that bears no fruit.

The speaker is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on what is worth pursuing in life. Tradition associates him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. In this passage he compares wisdom that reflects, even in the face of pain, with amusement that seeks only distraction. Thorns burn quickly and give a brief flame, without the lasting heat of good firewood.

For today: not everything that cheers us in the moment helps us grow. Enjoy wholesome laughter, but also seek sincere counsel and times of reflection that give firmness to your life.
exp.1:7:
The writer tells us that he gathered silver and gold, along with the treasures that once belonged to kings and to whole regions. He surrounded himself with male and female singers, with music and every kind of instrument, and with the pleasures people usually pursue.

The verse's word "gathered" is what the verse would call the sense of the phrase, and the "provinces" in the verse are the territories under his rule.

The one speaking is "the Preacher," who according to tradition is Solomon, though some scholars debate this. This man tested everything the world offers, looking to see whether wealth and pleasure could give meaning to life. Later he will conclude that, apart from God, all of it is empty.

Today we might ask ourselves: what am I accumulating, expecting it to make me feel complete? Good things are a gift, but they cannot take the place of God in the heart.
exp.3:11:
It says that a person alone is easier to overcome, but if there are two, they can defend themselves better. It then adds that a cord of three strands twisted together is not quickly broken. "Prevail against" means "overcome," and "not quickly" means "not swiftly." If someone attacks the one who is alone, two together stand against him.

The speaker is the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. Earlier he spoke of work done alone, with no one to share it with, and called that vanity. Now he shows the value of companionship: help, warmth, and protection. Some see in the "threefold cord" only an image of strength; others think of a third party, such as God, but the text does not say so.

Today, seek sincere friendships and a community of faith. Ask for help when you need it, and offer it when another falls. You do not have to carry everything by yourself.
exp.8:12:
It says the author saw another kind of wisdom in life, and that to him it seemed something important. "Under the sun" means in this world, as we see it day by day. It is the introduction to a story he tells right after.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just said that life is uncertain: speed, strength, or talent do not guarantee success, and bad times can fall suddenly. Now he presents a concrete example: a poor wise man saved a city, and no one remembered him.

For today: value wisdom even when it earns no applause. And recognize with gratitude the ordinary people who help quietly, without expecting fame.
exp.0:15:
He says he thought things over within himself. He saw himself as "great" in the sense of having more wisdom than all the rulers who had been before him in Jerusalem. His mind had received much wisdom and "learning," which here means knowledge.

The speaker is the Preacher, who presents himself as a king in Jerusalem and is traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has been examining life "under the sun" and concludes that everything is vanity, something fleeting. He is not boasting: he is showing that even the best human wisdom did not resolve the emptiness or the crookedness of this world.

For today: studying, learning, and getting ahead are good, but do not ask yourself to let knowledge fill your soul. Use what you know with humility and place your trust in God, who gives meaning to what wisdom alone cannot straighten out.
exp.0:2:
Here the Preacher asks a question: what real gain remains for a person after so much effort? The word "labour" in the verse means working hard, often with great weariness and worry. "Under the sun" means in this earthly life, as we see it and live it.

The one speaking is the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth), who presents himself as the son of David and king in Jerusalem. Many connect him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. After saying that everything is "vanity," meaning passing and fleeting like a breath, he asks whether human work leaves anything that lasts. The verses that follow illustrate this with generations that pass away and a sun that repeats its cycle.

Today we can work diligently, but without making work our god. If we place our work in God's hands and care for the people we love, our effort takes on a more lasting meaning.
exp.0:12:
Here the Preacher says that he resolved with all his effort to study and examine, using wisdom, everything that happens in life under the heavens, that is, in this world. He recognizes that God has given human beings a heavy and wearying task, that of occupying themselves with this search.

The Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth) presents himself as a king in Jerusalem. Many connect him with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He wants to show that even with wisdom and resources, trying to understand life on one's own leaves many questions unanswered.

For today: seek to understand life with wisdom, but accept that you will not know everything. Hand over to God what you do not understand, and trust Him in the midst of your questions.
exp.11:12:
It says that, after hearing everything that has been said in the book, the conclusion is simple: one must respect and honor God, and obey what He commands. "Discourse" means everything that has been spoken or taught. "Fear God" here means reverence and trust, not terror. "The whole of man" can be understood as the complete duty of the person, or what gives meaning to their life.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Ecclesiastes), who for a long time reflected on how empty life seems "under the sun." Here he closes the book with a conclusion. The verses before compare wise words to goads and nails: they guide and make firm. The next verse adds that God will judge every work, even what is hidden.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself: "Does this honor God?" Putting God first gives direction and peace to everything else.
exp.3:1:
It says the author considered the dead more fortunate than the living. Those who have already died are the ones who have passed on, and those who are still alive are the ones who still live. This is not advice to wish for death, but an expression of grief at what he was seeing.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qohelet in Hebrew. Tradition associates him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has just seen the violence and the tears of the oppressed, who had no one to comfort them. His sentence shows his anguish, not a direct teaching from God about death.

For today: do not ignore the suffering of others. Be the comforter that others do not have: listen, accompany, and help someone who is going through injustice or sadness.
exp.9:15:
It is a misfortune for a country when it is ruled by a "child" king, that is, one who is young, immature, or poorly prepared, and whose leaders begin the day with banquets, seeking pleasure instead of working. "Eating in the morning" speaks of feasting and excess from early hours. Some understand "child" as a person of few years; others, as someone of immature character.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, although not everyone agrees. In this passage he contrasts wisdom with folly. Earlier he spoke of fools who talk a great deal and do not know where they are going. Here he shows how poor leadership harms an entire people. The following verse gives the contrast: blessed is the land whose leaders are responsible and temperate.

For today: if you have any responsibility, at home, at work, or in the church, take care of your habits and priorities. And pray for those who govern, that they may act with maturity and self-control.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that being able to eat, drink, and enjoy the fruit of our labor is a gift from God. The phrase "enjoy the good of all his labour" means to take pleasure in what is good from our work.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who in the book reflects on the meaning of life. He is traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has just said that God makes everything beautiful in its time and that we cannot fully comprehend all of God's work. Faced with that mystery, he advises us to rejoice and do good, receiving everyday life with gratitude.

Today we can pause to give thanks for something simple: a meal, rest, or the fruit of our work. We do not need to understand everything in order to enjoy with gratitude what God gives us today.
exp.10:5:
It says we should sow early in the morning and keep working through the evening, without letting our hands sit idle. The reason is that we do not know which seed will bear fruit: this one, the other, or perhaps both.

The Preacher speaks, reflecting in Ecclesiastes on the meaning and limits of life. Just before this, he says that whoever waits for perfect weather never sows or reaps, and that we do not understand the ways of God, just as we do not understand the wind or the mystery of birth. For this reason he advises us to act with diligence, even though we do not control the outcome.

For today: do not wait until you have all the answers or perfect conditions to begin. Faithfully do the good that is within your reach, whether it is work, service, teaching, or helping others, and entrust the results to God, who knows what you do not know.
exp.6:22:
He says that the writer tested all these things by means of wisdom. He set out to become wise, but felt that wisdom was moving away from him, that is, that he did not fully attain it. "I proved" means I examined or investigated, and the phrase "I will be wise" means "I am going to be wise."

The Preacher speaks, called Qohelet, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. It comes from a call to humility: no one is perfect, and all of us have spoken badly of others. Then he admits that wisdom has limits, because there are deep things that human beings cannot comprehend.

For today: recognize that you do not know everything. Seek to understand with effort, but rest in God when something is beyond you. That humility will help you learn more and judge others less.
exp.9:11:
It says that what comes out of a wise person's mouth is pleasing and does good to others. The fool, on the other hand, by his own words, sinks and destroys himself. "Grace" here means something pleasant, kind, and uplifting. "Ruin" means destruction or downfall.

The book attributes these words to "the Preacher," traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. In this passage it reflects on practical wisdom. Earlier it spoke of the serpent that bites and of the "babbler," that is, the gossip or chatterer, who is no better. Then it describes the fool who talks a great deal and without direction, beginning with foolishness and ending in harmful madness.

Before you speak, ask yourself a simple question: will what I am about to say help or hurt? Asking God to guard your words, and sometimes keeping silent, can spare you trouble and bless those who listen to you.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that what happens today has already happened before, and what is yet to come has also already taken place in some way. The last phrase, "Dios restaura lo que pasó," can be understood in several ways: that God brings back what has already been lived, or that God seeks out and remembers what was pursued or left behind. Translators do not agree on this.

The Preacher, or Qohelet, speaks here, reflecting on the passing of time. He has just said that what God does is lasting and that we should fear Him. Shortly afterward he speaks of injustice on the earth and affirms that God will judge everyone.

Today we can rest in the fact that God remains in control of time and of history. If something unjust or painful from the past weighs on you, place it in His hands, and enjoy with gratitude what He gives you today.
exp.7:11:
It says that although a wicked person does evil a hundred times and God is slow to punish them, the writer knows that it will go well for those who fear God. "Prolonged" means delayed or extended. "Fear God" does not mean being afraid, but respecting Him and living with reverence before Him.

The one speaking is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He observes that life seems unfair: the wicked prosper and the righteous are forgotten. Even so, he affirms with faith that the fear of God in the end bears good fruit. That tension between what he sees and what he believes runs through the whole passage.

For today: when you see someone unjust doing well, do not become bitter or imitate their path. Keep acting with uprightness and trust that God is just, even when His timing is not yours.
exp.4:2:
It says that just as too much work and worry fill the mind and produce dreams, so too talking too much exposes the fool. The words "business" and "multitude of words" are rendered as they appear in the verse above: "business" refers to busy activity and anxious labor, and "multitude of words" refers to speaking without restraint. The fool's voice is recognized because he talks a great deal and thinks little.

The one speaking in Ecclesiastes is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who is traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate his identity. Here he teaches how to draw near to God. Before and after this verse, he warns against hasty words and empty promises in worship.

For today: before you pray, make a promise, or speak in church, pause. Listen first. Say few words to God, but sincere ones, and keep what you say. A quiet heart prays better than a hasty mouth.
exp.8:4:
It says that the living at least know they will die one day, but the dead no longer know anything about what happens in this world.

The Preacher (Qohélet) speaks here, and he is traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He reflects on life "under the sun," that is, from what can be seen in this world. He does not try to describe everything that happens after death, but to show that present life is brief and precious. That is why right after this he invites people to enjoy with gratitude what God gives.

For today: do not put off what is important. Love, forgive, work honestly, and thank God today, while you still have time and life.
exp.1:12:
It says that wisdom is far better than folly, just as light is better than darkness. "Surpasses" means that it exceeds or outdoes. Folly is a lack of understanding, living without thinking or listening to God.

The author of Ecclesiastes, called "the Preacher," is traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has tested work, pleasures, and achievements, and all of them seem empty to him. Even so, he recognizes that wisdom has real value. But he quickly admits that death comes to the wise and the foolish alike, and that troubles him.

For today: seek wisdom in your daily decisions, asking God for direction before you act. It is worth it, even though it does not solve everything. Its light helps you walk better, and your ultimate hope rests in God.
exp.4:12:
It speaks of a painful and grievous evil that the author has seen "under the sun," that is, in this life: riches that their owner hoards and that end up doing them harm. The phrase about a painful sickness refers to an affliction that causes great distress. The phrase about harm to the owner means that what is kept turns against him.

The speaker is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has been reflecting on the emptiness of living for money. Earlier he showed that more possessions bring more expenses and more worries, and that the rich man does not sleep peacefully. Afterward he will say that such riches can be lost and that no one takes anything with them when they die.

For today: ask yourself whether your money serves you or whether you serve it. Practice being generous and content with what you have, and trust God more than your savings, so that you can sleep in peace.
exp.11:5:
This verse uses four everyday images: a silver cord that snaps, a golden bowl that cracks, a pitcher that breaks at the spring, and a wheel that shatters over the well. The opening word signals that these things will happen soon. Many understand them as pictures of death, when what is precious and fragile in life gives way. Some connect them with the human body, but not everyone agrees on what each image represents.

The Preacher (Ecclesiastes) speaks to the young and urges them to remember their Creator before old age and death arrive. The verses before it describe aging with poetic images, and the one after it says that the dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God.

Today: do not put off what matters most. Live with gratitude and seek God now, while you still have strength, caring for your relationship with Him and with those you love.
exp.6:10:
It says that knowledge is good when it goes together with an inheritance, that is, with possessions or resources. And it is even more beneficial for "those who see the sun," a poetic way of saying those who are alive. In this older version, "knowledge" means understanding or practical wisdom. Some translations read "as good as an inheritance," and scholars debate which meaning is correct.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some question this. He is reflecting on how to live well in this brief life. The next verse says that both wisdom and money offer protection, but wisdom gives life.

For today: value both learning and material things, but do not put them in the highest place. Use what you have and what you know wisely and gratefully, while you have life, and seek God above all.
exp.7:9:
The writer says he saw something unjust: wicked people were buried with honor and are still remembered with respect, while people who walked in the holy place and acted rightly were soon forgotten, right in the city where they had done good. The ones he calls "wicked" are those who live without fear of God. And he concludes that this too is futility, meaning something that cannot be understood or resolved, like a breath of wind.

The Teacher of Ecclesiastes speaks as one who observes life "under the sun," and he is perplexed by things that seem unjust. Yet the passage that follows affirms that it will go well in the end for those who fear God. Some scholars note that the Hebrew text of this verse is difficult and is translated in several different ways.

Today we can serve God and do good without expecting applause or remembrance from people. Our worth does not depend on fame, but on the fact that God sees and remembers every faithful act.
exp.5:5:
It says that even if someone lived two thousand years (a thousand years, twice over), if he was unable to enjoy the good things of life, in the end he ends up the same as everyone else. "That one" is the person being spoken of, and "a place" refers to the grave, the tomb. "Enjoyed the good" means having taken pleasure in the good that God gives.

The Preacher is speaking, and in Ecclesiastes he reflects on what he calls "vanity," the fleeting nature of life. He has just been speaking about a child born dead, and he says that this child rests better than a rich man who never enjoyed what he had. It is a harsh comparison, and scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: having years, money, or achievements is not enough if we never learn to be thankful. Today, enjoy a meal, your family, or your work with gratitude, and remember that all of it is a gift from God.
exp.11:2:
He says that, as a person grows old, the body gradually weakens. "The keepers of the house" are usually understood as the arms and hands that tremble. "The strong men who bow themselves" would be the legs or the back. "The grinders" are the teeth, which are lost and no longer suffice for chewing. "Those that look out of the windows" would be the eyes, which see less and less. "Shall cease" means "shall stop working."

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He uses a poetic image: the body as a house that is falling into disrepair. He says this to encourage young people to remember their Creator before the difficult years arrive.

For today: do not put off your relationship with God. Today, with the strength you have, devote time to prayer, to the Bible, and to serving others.
exp.1:15:
It says that neither the wise person nor the foolish one will be remembered forever. As time passes, everything is forgotten, and in the end both die the same way. The verse of the words "happen" and "futility" has been removed here, since neither word appears in the verse your readers see.

The Preacher speaks, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has sought meaning in wisdom, riches, and labor. He recognizes that wisdom is better than foolishness, but he is frustrated because death reaches everyone and fame fades away. So he feels weariness and discouragement.

For today: do not place your worth in being remembered or in your achievements. All of that is temporary. Live with humility, do your work well, and place it in God's hands, who does give meaning and does not forget his own.
exp.0:16:
He says the author gave himself wholeheartedly to know wisdom, and also to understand madness and folly, that is, foolishness and senseless ideas. "Vexation of spirit" means something like chasing the wind: weariness of the soul, without managing to catch what one is seeking.

The one speaking is the "Preacher" of Ecclesiastes, who presents himself as a king in Jerusalem; tradition usually thinks of Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He recounts his search for meaning "under the sun," using only reason and experience. He concludes that human knowledge, by itself, does not straighten what is crooked or give full peace.

For today: study, learn, and seek to understand life, but do not expect knowledge alone to fill your heart. Lay your questions before God, trusting that He sustains what you cannot explain.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that the words of the wise are like goads, the pointed sticks used to guide oxen and make them move forward. They are also like nails firmly driven in, steady and secure. These words come from masters of the assemblies, and they were "given by one Shepherd." Many understand that this Shepherd is God himself, though some think it refers to Solomon or another leader.

The speaker is the Preacher, who closes his book in Ecclesiastes. He has just said that he sought pleasing words that were also true. Now he explains that right wisdom pricks, pushes, and gives firmness. He then warns that one should not get lost in endless books, but should arrive at what is essential: fearing God.

For today: do not seek only ideas that make you feel good. Let the Word of God push you to change and give you firmness. Choose one verse today and put it into practice.
exp.2:7:
This verse names two pairs of opposites: loving and hating, war and peace. "Hating" means feeling strong rejection or aversion toward something. The text does not command us to hate or to make war; it recognizes that life holds very different moments.

The speaker is "the Preacher," traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. His list of times shows that life has seasons we do not fully control. He then asks what profit a person gains from so much toil, and says that God has given us work and limits.

For today: before you react, ask yourself what season you are living in. Ask God for wisdom to know when to care, when to stand up for what is right, and when to seek peace. You can trust that He sustains your seasons.
exp.9:5:
He says that sometimes fools end up in the highest positions, while the rich, or people who are capable and valuable, are left in humble places. "Folly" is lack of wisdom. "Rich" can refer to money, but also to people of noble standing or worth. The world seems turned upside down.

The one speaking is the Preacher, the teacher of Ecclesiastes, who observes life "under the sun." He has just spoken of an angry ruler, and now he points to an evil he has seen: mistakes by leaders who put people in the wrong places. The next verse confirms this with the image of servants on horseback and princes walking on foot.

For today: when you see injustice or foolish leadership, do not grow bitter or react in haste. Stay calm, be upright, and trust that God sees what you see. And if you have authority, seek wisdom before appearance.
exp.4:3:
It says that if you make a promise to God, do not delay in keeping it. "Fools" are people who speak without thinking and do not take their words seriously. "Pay" here means to carry out what was promised. God is not pleased when someone promises and then forgets.

The book is traditionally attributed to Solomon, although some scholars debate who wrote it. The speaker presents himself as "the Preacher" and gives advice on how to approach God with reverence. First he asks for few words, because God is great and we are small. Promises made to God, such as vows or commitments in worship, were taken very seriously in Israel.

For today: before you say to God "I promise," think carefully about what you can actually keep. And if you have already promised something good, set a date and carry it out, whether it is serving, helping, or giving up a bad habit.
exp.6:26:
Here the Preacher says that what he is about to tell was found with great care. "Weighing the things one by one" is like placing each idea on a scale, without rushing, in order to find "the account," that is, the meaning or explanation of things.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), who throughout the book searches for the meaning of life. Earlier he spoke of a bitter experience with a woman who trapped him, and then he says he did not find what he was looking for. Many read this as a warning against deceit and temptation, not as a judgment on all women. He ends by saying that God made man upright, but people have complicated things for themselves.

For today: before drawing conclusions, examine things calmly and humbly. Ask God for wisdom, and do not let yourself be carried away by whatever captures your heart.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that people forget what happened before us, and that those who come after us will also not remember what we do.

The text speaks of "the Preacher," who in the book is presented as a son of David and a king in Jerusalem. Many associate him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this.
