He reflects on life "under the sun," that is, viewed only from a human perspective. That is why he says that "there is nothing new": everything seems to repeat itself and is forgotten with time.

For today: do not place your worth in being remembered or in your achievements. Do with love and faithfulness what God gives you today, because He does know your life and your work, even when others forget it.
exp.1:21:
This verse is a question: what does a person gain from all their work and from the anxious concern of their heart, the striving they carry on under the sun? The sense is that the answer is: very little.

The Preacher of Ecclesiastes speaks here, and he is traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate who wrote it. He has just said that he may have to leave everything he achieved to someone who did not work for it. That is why he feels discouraged. Later, however, he points out that enjoying the good things of life is a gift from God's hand.

Today we can work diligently without living enslaved to worry. Take time to rest, give thanks, and simply enjoy what God gives you, like a meal with your family.
exp.7:12:
It will not go well for the wicked person in the end, and his life will not be lengthened; his days pass quickly, like a shadow. The reason is that he had no fear of God. "Fear" here does not mean being frightened, but respecting God and living knowing that he sees us. The one who lives without taking God into account is the one who lacks this fear.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Ecclesiastes), who observes life under the sun. He has just said that punishment sometimes takes a long time to come, and that it seems the wicked prosper. Even so, he affirms his conviction that God has the final word. But he soon admits that life does not always look so just, and for that reason he speaks of vanity. Some read this as a firm hope, others as a tension that he leaves open.

For today: when you see someone doing harm and seeming to get away with it, do not become bitter or imitate them. Live with respect for God in everyday life, trust that he sees and judges with justice, and enjoy with gratitude the good that he gives you today.
exp.4:10:
It says that when someone has more wealth, the people who live off of it also increase: employees, relatives, friends, and people who take advantage. The "eaters" the verse speaks of are those who consume or spend those goods. So what does the owner gain? Almost nothing, only the sight of his money going away before his eyes, watching it pass without being able to hold on to it.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Ecclesiastes), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He is reflecting on the vanity, or emptiness, of loving money. He says that whoever loves it is never satisfied, and the following verse contrasts the rich man who lies awake with the worker who sleeps peacefully.

For today: do not place your security in having more. Learn to give thanks for what you have, to share generously, and to seek the peace that God gives, which money cannot buy.
exp.0:1:
He says that everything is "vanity," and he repeats the word to give it more force. "Vanity of vanities" is a way of saying "the emptiest thing of all." "Preacher" comes from Qoheleth, who speaks before an assembly.

The speaker is the Preacher, presented as the son of David and king in Jerusalem. Many think he is Solomon, though some scholars debate this. From the start, he reflects on how brief and limited life is "under the sun," that is, without looking beyond this world.

For today: do not place your final security in achievements, money, or fame, because they pass away like vapor. Enjoy with gratitude what God gives you, but rest in Him.
exp.1:6:
He says he had many male and female servants, and also servants who were born in his house. Besides this, he had huge herds of cattle and sheep, more than anyone who had ruled in Jerusalem before him.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), who presents himself as a son of David, king in Jerusalem. Many believe he is Solomon, although some scholars think he is a wise voice who uses that figure. He describes an experiment: he tested riches, pleasures, and achievements to see whether they gave life meaning. He then concludes that all of that, on its own, is fleeting.

For today: enjoy what God gives you with gratitude, but do not place your security or your purpose in your possessions. Ask yourself which things truly fill you and which ones only distract you.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the human being does not know what will happen in the future, and that no one can tell him when it will occur. "What is to come" means what will come, and "the time when it will be" refers to the exact moment. We have no way of knowing the future on our own.

The author of Ecclesiastes, called "the Preacher" (Qoheleth), is speaking. Tradition associates him with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. In this passage he reflects on wisdom, authority, and God's judgment. He says that the wise person understands there is a proper time for everything, but that human beings are limited: they do not control the future or the day of their death, as the following verses explain.

For today: make plans with prudence, but do not live anxious about what you cannot know. Obey God in what is before you today and place tomorrow in His hands, because He does know what is to come.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that the author made gardens and orchards for himself and planted in them trees of every kind of fruit. The word "made" here means that he built or created these for himself. "Orchards" are plots of land with fruit trees, and "gardens" are cultivated spaces meant to be enjoyed for their beauty.

The speaker of Ecclesiastes, who calls himself the Preacher, presents himself as a king in Jerusalem. Tradition holds that he is Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. In this passage he recounts an experiment: testing pleasures, works, and riches to discover what gives true meaning to life "under the sun." His projects are grand, but later he will conclude that all of these things, on their own, do not fill the heart.

Today we can enjoy with gratitude the good things God gives us, such as nature, work, and rest. But we should not expect these things to give us life's ultimate meaning. That is found only in God.
exp.9:19:
It says not to speak badly of the king, not even in your thoughts, nor of the rich, even when you are alone in your room. The reason is that "the birds of the air" and "those that have wings" will carry the message. It is a figure of speech: what you say in secret can come to light. "Room" is the private chamber, and "voice" and "word" refer to what you said.

The author is the Preacher, called Qoheleth (tradition links him to Solomon, though some scholars dispute this). In this chapter he gives advice on practical wisdom, folly, and living under authority. Here he warns that criticizing the powerful can bring consequences, and that what is secret is discovered more easily than we think.

For today: take care with your words, even when you think no one can hear you. You can express disagreement with respect and through good means, without gossip or contempt, trusting that God sees the heart.
exp.6:18:
This verse says that wisdom gives more strength to the one who has it than ten rulers or leaders with power give to a city. "Strengthens" means it gives firmness and protection. "Mighty men" refers to men with authority or military power, and "which are in the city" means they were located in that city.

The Preacher, or Qoheleth, speaks, who according to tradition is Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He comes from warning against extremes: not being wicked or foolish, and fearing God. Right away he recognizes that no one is perfectly righteous. Wisdom appears as a real help for living with balance, even while we are imperfect.

For today: before looking for security only in money, connections, or power, ask God for wisdom and practice it. Think before you act, listen to counsel, and acknowledge your limits with humility. That will sustain you more than any human support.
exp.7:8:
He says that the author has carefully observed everything that happens in this life "under the sun," that is, in the world as we see it. And he has noticed that there are times when one person rules over another, and that this rule ends up doing harm to the one ruled. The verse's wording "ruleth over" means to lord it over others with authority. Harm may fall on the victim, and many understand that it also falls on the one who oppresses.

The Preacher speaks, called Qoheleth, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He reflects on life with its injustices and limits. He has just said that no one has power over the day of death. In this way he shows that human power is limited and that abuses do not have the final word.

Today, if you have authority at home, at work, or in the church, use it to serve and not to dominate. Remember that one day you will give an account to God.
exp.11:11:
This verse is advice from a father to his son: "Be careful, be wise." It says there is never an end to writing books, and that studying too much wears out the body. "Further, by these" means "furthermore, by these"; "be admonished" is "be warned" or "pay attention." "Weariness of the flesh" means physical exhaustion.

The Preacher (Qoheleth), the teacher who closes the book of Ecclesiastes, is speaking. Earlier he praised the words of the wise, which guide like goads, and which come from one Shepherd. Now he warns that no amount of human books can replace that wisdom. His conclusion comes right after: fear God and keep his commandments.

For today: there is information without limit, and we cannot keep up with everything. Before filling yourself with opinions, read the Bible calmly, pray, and practice what you learn. Rest without guilt and seek wisdom that brings you closer to God.
exp.1:23:
It says that the best thing a person can do is enjoy the simple things of each day: eating, drinking, and taking satisfaction in their work. It adds that this ability to enjoy does not come from oneself but is a gift "from the hand of God." The sense of the phrase about seeing good in one's labour means that the person finds joy in the fruit of their effort.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qohelet, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. After searching for meaning in wealth, wisdom, and pleasure, he sees that everything is fleeting, like vapor. Here he does not recommend living without purpose, but receiving with gratitude what God gives.

Today, pause in your day to thank God for your food and for your work, without living only in a hurry and in anxiety.
exp.5:10:
It says that talking a lot solves nothing; on the contrary, it increases what is empty and useless. "Vanity" here does not mean pride, but something fleeting, like a vapor that cannot be caught. The question "What more does a man have?" means: what real advantage does someone gain from so many words and arguments?

The Preacher, called Qoheleth, traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this, speaks. He has just said that no one can argue with God, who is stronger. He reflects that human arguments do not change what God has determined, nor do they give us answers about the future.

For today: before you argue, give your opinion, or complain, stop and ask yourself whether your words add anything good. Speak less, listen more, and bring your questions to God with humility and trust.
exp.1:11:
Here the author says he turned again to examine three things: wisdom, madness (senseless thoughts and ideas), and folly (living without judgment). He then asks what someone could do who comes after the king, and suggests that no one will be able to do anything very different from what he has already tried.

The Preacher of Ecclesiastes speaks, presenting himself as a king in Jerusalem; traditionally he is identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. After testing pleasures and great works without finding lasting satisfaction, he now compares wisdom with folly. His conclusion will come shortly: wisdom is better, but even it does not prevent death.

For today: do not expect success, pleasure or knowledge to fill your life completely. Seek wisdom, but put it at the service of God, who gives meaning beyond what we achieve.
exp.8:8:
This verse invites you to enjoy life with the wife you love during the brief days God gives you in this world. "Vanity" here does not mean pride but something passing, like a breath that quickly disappears. The text says that enjoying your marriage and your work is "your portion," that is, what has been given to you to receive.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on the meaning of life "under the sun," that is, from what we see in this world. Tradition associates him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. Since death comes to everyone and much is uncertain, he advises receiving God's simple gifts with gratitude.

For today: set aside time this week to truly enjoy your spouse, or a loved one if you are not married, without rushing or checking your phone, giving thanks to God for that gift.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked. The author says it to himself, "in my heart." He affirms that there is a time set by God for every purpose and for every work. The phrase "for every matter or desire" explains the meaning of the words "for every purpose." "Wicked" refers to someone who lives without regard for God.

The author is Qoheleth, the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, who is traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He has just seen that in places of justice there is wickedness. That injustice grieves him, and he finds comfort in the fact that God has the final word. Then he reflects on death, which reaches everyone.

Today, when you see injustice and feel powerless, do not become bitter or seek revenge. Do what is right, pray, and trust that God sees everything and will judge in his time.
exp.2:13:
This verse says that God's works last forever and are complete: nothing can be added to them or taken away from them. The word for "forever" means it remains. The verse's wording on what God does is, in plain terms, "whatever God does." The word for "fear" here speaks of respect and reverence before God, not of terror.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just said that there is a time for everything and that enjoying work and food is a gift from God. Now he concludes that, while our plans change, what God decides remains. That invites us to humility.

For today: instead of worrying about controlling everything, rest in the fact that God sustains what is essential. Enjoy everyday things with gratitude, such as your food and your work, and live with reverence toward Him.
exp.7:15:
Here the author says that he set his whole heart to learn wisdom and to observe the work and the restless labor of people on the earth. He mentions that there are people who neither by day nor by night know sleep, that is, they do not rest because they are so busy.

The author of Ecclesiastes, called "the Preacher" or Qohelet, speaks here. Tradition connects him with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He has just shown that life seems unjust and confusing. Now he tries to understand it and concludes that no one can grasp all that God does.

For today: do not live worn out by wanting to control and understand everything. Work diligently, but rest, enjoy the good that God gives you, and trust Him where you do not understand.
exp.2:5:
It says that in life there are times to gain and times to lose, times to keep things and times to let them go. The word "get" is about gaining or acquiring something, such as earning or building up possessions. "Cast away" is about throwing out what no longer serves or is no longer wise to keep.

The one speaking is the author of Ecclesiastes, called "the Preacher" or Qoheleth. Tradition links him with Solomon, though some scholars question this. This poem about times shows that life has rhythms we do not fully control. In this way, the writer invites us to accept with wisdom that God governs the times.

Today we can learn to let go without bitterness. If you go through a loss, such as a job, money, or a season of life, it does not mean that everything is lost. Ask God for wisdom to know what to keep and what to let go, and trust that he sustains you in every season.
exp.1:19:
He says that the author once again became completely discouraged. Looking at all the effort of his life, carried out with wisdom, he felt that it had not given him a firm hope. The word "turned" in the verse expresses this turning of his heart, and "despair" means to lose hope or spirit. The word "labour" refers to hard work.

The Preacher speaks, whom many identify with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He reflects on life "under the sun," that is, looking only at what is earthly. It grieves him that everything he built will pass to someone who does not know whether that person will be wise or foolish, and who did not work for it.

For today: work with care, but do not place all your hope in your work or your achievements. Offer it to God, enjoy what He gives you, and trust that the most valuable part of your life does not depend only on what you leave on this earth.
exp.3:15:
It says that the crowd following the young king was countless, yet the generations that come after will not rejoice in him. People applaud today and forget tomorrow. That is why the author calls it "vanity," something that vanishes, and "vexation of spirit," a striving that wears out the soul, like chasing the wind.

The one speaking is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some dispute this. He observes life "under the sun" and notes that even a wise young man who rises to the throne loses popular esteem over time.

Today we can learn not to base our worth on applause or fame. People's opinions change. Let us seek first to please God and serve faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.2:8:
This verse is a question: what does a person gain who works so hard at their labor? The word "profit" means lasting gain or benefit. It does not say that work is bad, but asks what remains in the end after so much effort.

The speaker is the author of Ecclesiastes, who presents himself as the Teacher. Tradition links him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has just said that there is a time for everything in life, and now he asks whether our striving changes those times. The verses that follow answer: God ordains everything, and we do not see the whole picture.

For today: work diligently, but do not place the whole meaning of your life in your work. Hand your plans over to God, rest in the fact that He governs the times, and seek to enjoy what He gives you with gratitude.
exp.0:17:
It says that the more wisdom a person has, the more worries they carry, and that whoever increases their knowledge also increases their sorrow. "Grief" means heaviness of heart or vexation, and "knowledge" means what is learned and understood.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who presents himself as king in Jerusalem. Tradition identifies him with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He sought to understand life with his wisdom, and also folly, but he discovered that knowing more did not take away his anguish. Seeing the world more clearly showed him more injustice and limits.

Today, knowing more can make us feel more keenly the weight of the world's problems. We should not stop learning, but we should remember that knowledge alone does not give peace. We can bring what we know and what hurts us to God in prayer, trusting that He understands what we cannot grasp.
exp.3:2:
It says that, seeing so much injustice in the world, it is better not to have been born at all than to see the evil that is done "under the sun", that is, in this earthly life. "Some and others" refers to the dead and the living he spoke of before. "Better" in this verse means "more to be preferred" (the word "better" as it appears in the verse above).

The Preacher speaks, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has just seen oppression: people weeping with no one to comfort them, while the powerful abuse. His conclusion is bitter and deliberately exaggerated. It does not teach a lesson about the value of life; it expresses the honest pain of someone who looks at the world without hope from above.

For today: do not close your eyes to the suffering of others or grow used to it. Be the comfort that this text longs for: visit, listen, help, or defend someone who is suffering, trusting that God does see and does comfort.
exp.5:9:
It says that whatever exists has already been named and has its purpose from long ago, and that a human being is simply what he is: a man, with limits. For that reason he cannot argue with, or fight against, someone stronger than himself. In context, that stronger one is usually understood to be God.

The one speaking is the Teacher, or Qoheleth, who reflects on how brief and limited life is under the sun. He has just said that neither the wise person nor the poor person escapes frustration. Here he adds that arguing with God about what we do not understand accomplishes nothing. Some read this as an invitation to humility, others as a more resigned tone.

For today: when something in your life has no explanation, instead of fighting with God or demanding answers, you can bring Him your questions with humility and trust that He knows more than you do.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that life has opposite moments, and each one arrives in its time. The verse speaks of killing and healing, and of breaking down and building up. Some of the old words in the context: "a time" in the verse refers to the right moment for each thing, and mourning is lamenting over someone who has died.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who presents himself as the son of David, king in Jerusalem. Tradition holds that this is Solomon, though some scholars dispute it. With this poem he shows that life has rhythms we do not fully control. The verse does not approve of all violence; it describes the reality of a fallen world.

For today: not every moment calls for the same thing. If you are in a season of grief or collapse, trust that God also has a time to heal and rebuild. Ask him for wisdom to know what needs to be done now.
exp.1:2:
He says the writer decided to treat his body to wine, that is, to indulge himself and be good to his body through drink. Even so, he wanted his heart to stay guided by wisdom, and so he says he kept hold of wisdom while going after folly, so that he would not fall into madness. His aim was to discover what is truly good that people can do during the few days of their lives under the heaven.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who is traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He runs an experiment: he tests pleasure, works, and riches to see whether they give meaning to life. Later he concludes that, without God, all of that is vanity, something fleeting.

For today: enjoy with gratitude what God gives you, but do not expect pleasure to fill your life. Put God and his wisdom first.
exp.8:0:
Here the author says he devoted himself to thinking deeply about everything he has observed in life. His conclusion is that the righteous and the wise, along with what they do, are in the hand of God. He also says that by looking at what happens to a person, no one can know whether God loves them or rejects them.

The Preacher, called Qoheleth, speaks here, and he is traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He reflects on life as it is lived under the sun and notes that good people and bad people can experience the same things, including death. For this reason he acknowledges the limits of our understanding.

For today: when life seems unfair or confusing, do not measure God's love only by what happens to you. Keep doing good, and rest in the knowledge that you and your future are in God's hands, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that people and animals share the same end in death: the body returns to the earth. "All go to one place" means that everyone ends up in the same place, the grave. It is a reminder that God formed man from the dust (Genesis 2:7; 3:19).

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He observes life only from what can be seen, "under the sun," and concludes that death levels everyone. He describes life as fleeting, like a breath or vapor. He himself asks who knows what happens to the spirit, and other passages of Scripture offer more hope.

For today: since our life is brief, let us live with humility, thankful to God, enjoying the good of each day and not setting our hearts on what does not last.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that it is better not to make a vow to God than to make one and then fail to keep it.

The book of Ecclesiastes is attributed to "the Preacher," traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. In this passage, he advises how to approach God in worship: with reverence, few words, and sincerity. He warns against vows made lightly, which can end in shame and in losing what a person has worked for.

Before you commit yourself to God or to others, think carefully about whether you will truly be able to keep your word. It is better to speak few words and keep them than to promise a great deal in a moment of emotion and then fail.
exp.7:10:
It says that when punishment for wickedness is slow to come, people are encouraged to keep doing evil. "Sentence" is the judgment or punishment, and "speedily" means quickly. "Fully set in them" means the heart becomes filled with courage and determination to do wrong.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He observes the injustices of life "under the sun": the wicked seem to get away with it and are even remembered with honor. He does not approve of this; he calls it vanity. But he immediately affirms that things will go well for those who fear God.

For today: do not mistake God's patience for indifference. If you have done wrong and nothing has happened, do not take it as permission. Use that time to repent and live with reverence for God.
exp.10:3:
It says that whoever keeps watching the wind to know whether it is a good time never sows, and whoever spends the day looking at the clouds never harvests. In other words, waiting for perfect conditions can leave us doing nothing. The verse's word "reap" means to gather in a harvest, and "sow" means to plant seed.

The book is traditionally attributed to Solomon, though some scholars debate who wrote it. Here the Teacher (Qoheleth) teaches that we cannot control or predict what is coming. Since we do not know what will happen, we should not freeze in fear. We should trust God, who does all things, and work with generosity and diligence.

For today: if you are waiting for everything to feel safe before taking a step, such as starting a project, serving others, or forgiving someone, take one small action today and entrust the outcome to God.
exp.3:5:
It says that it is better to have little, but with calm, than to have much at the cost of an exhausting life full of anguish. "A handful" is a hand with just enough; "both hands full" is abundance. "Quietness" is stillness or peace, and "vexation of spirit" is restlessness of the soul, like chasing the wind.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate his authorship. He has just said that much labor comes from envy between neighbors. Before this verse he mentions the fool who folds his arms and ruins himself. Here he proposes a middle way: neither laziness nor excessive ambition.

For today: ask yourself whether your effort has a healthy limit. Set aside a fixed time each week to rest and to thank God for what you already have, instead of comparing yourself with others.
exp.2:21:
It says that the best thing a person can do is enjoy the fruit of their labor, because that is their portion in life. No one can bring them back after death to show them what will happen on earth once they are gone. The phrase "what he shall do" is the same idea as "what he does," and "his portion" means his share or what falls to him.

The Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some dispute this, speaks here. He has just said that people and animals return to dust, and that death is uncertain and limits us. So he concludes that life is brief, and that enjoying it with gratitude is a gift from God, not a goal that explains everything.

For today: value and enjoy your work, your food, and your family with gratitude, without living anxiously trying to control the future. Do well what is in front of you today, and entrust tomorrow to God.
exp.8:5:
It says that when a person dies, their feelings come to an end: their love, their hatred, and their envy are now gone. The word "perished" in the verse is the one used here to mean that they have come to an end. The word "age" or "world" in the original refers to the present life. The dead no longer take part in anything that happens "under the sun," that is, in this earthly life.

The Preacher, or Qoheleth, speaks as he reflects on life from what can be seen in this world. His point is that death comes to everyone and that only the living have the chance to act. For that reason, he goes on to invite readers to enjoy God's gifts with gratitude. Some scholars see here only a limited human viewpoint; others see a truth about the end of our earthly life.

For today: do not leave what is important for later. If you hold a grudge, make peace. If you should say "I love you," say it today, while you still have time.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that the author has reached the conclusion that the best thing people can do is to rejoice and do good while they live. "To do good in one's life" can be understood as acting with kindness, or as enjoying the good things of life. Scholars interpret it both ways, and perhaps it includes both ideas.

The one speaking is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some dispute this. He has just said that God makes everything beautiful in its time and that we cannot understand all his work. Faced with that mystery, he does not propose worrying, but receiving life with gratitude, as a gift from God.

For today: do not wait until you understand everything before living with joy. Today, give thanks for something simple, like a meal or a conversation, and do one concrete good for someone close to you.
exp.11:1:
It says that people should remember God before old age arrives, described as a time when the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars are darkened, and the clouds come back after the rain. The word "return" in the verse means "come back." It is a poetic image: life is slowly fading, and troubles seem never to end, like storms that keep coming back.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. Here he advises young people. After reflecting on how fleeting life is, he invites them to honor their Creator early. The verses that follow continue with images of the aging body: hands that tremble, eyesight that clouds over, hearing that fails.

For today: do not put off your relationship with God. Today itself, set aside a few minutes to pray, read the Bible, and give thanks to him, without waiting until you have more time or fewer problems.
exp.7:0:
It says that there is no one like the wise person, someone who understands the meaning of things. That wisdom shows on the outside: it makes the face shine and changes the harshness of the countenance, that is, its hardness or roughness.

The one speaking is the Preacher, the author of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. After reflecting on life and its puzzles, he praises wisdom. The verses that follow apply it to a specific case: how to behave with humility and respect before the authority of the king.

For today: ask God for understanding before you react. If, when faced with a problem or a difficult authority, you pause, listen, and think calmly, your attitude softens, and that also shows in your face and in how you treat others.
exp.0:3:
It says that people are born and die, one generation leaves and another arrives, but the earth remains there, firm. "Remains" means that it continues, that it does not disappear. The word "but" is the word that connects the two ideas.

The speaker is the Preacher, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, although some scholars think he was another wise man. He reflects on life "under the sun," that is, looking only at what is earthly. He asks what benefit remains from so much effort, and he points out that nature keeps its cycles while we pass by quickly.

For today: our life is brief, so it is wise not to set our hearts only on achievements that come to an end. Spend time on what lasts: loving God, caring for your family, and serving others with gratitude and simplicity.
exp.11:4:
It says that in old age a person is afraid of heights, and walking becomes risky because of stumbling. The almond tree blossoms (its flowers are white, and many see it as an image of gray hair). The grasshopper becomes a weight, and appetite or desire is lost.

The one speaking is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, who counsels the young. Just before this passage he tells them to remember their Creator in their youth. He describes aging with poetic images, and some of them are understood in several ways.

For today: don't wait until you have little strength to seek God. Today you can pray, serve him, and thank him for each day of life. And if you are already older, God is still with you.
exp.6:4:
It is better to hear a correction from a wise person, even when it stings, than to listen to the songs of fools, which sound pleasant but do not help. "Rebuke" means correction or a warning. "Fools" are people who refuse to learn or to think about the consequences.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on how to live well in a world full of limits and pain. Many believe it is Solomon, although the book does not say so clearly. In this passage he compares what pleases us with what helps us grow. The next verse says that the laughter of a fool is like thorns crackling under a pot: much noise, little heat, and nothing that lasts.

Today, instead of surrounding ourselves only with people who applaud us, we can look for a wise and sincere person, and receive their advice with humility, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.9:18:
This verse says that people hold feasts to enjoy themselves and be glad, and that wine lifts the spirits of those who live. It then adds that "money answereth all things," meaning that with money many needs get resolved.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some dispute this. He comes from speaking of rulers who eat at the proper time and of the laziness that ruins a house. Some believe the verse describes realistically how life works; others think it speaks with irony, showing a very limited view of what matters.

For today: enjoy food and joy with gratitude, but do not place your trust in money as if it solved everything. Money helps, but it does not heal the heart or give meaning to life. Use it wisely and generously.
exp.1:10:
He says the author stopped to look at everything he had made with his hands and the effort it had cost him. His conclusion is that all of it was vanity, that is, something fleeting and empty, like a breath of air. He also calls it vexation of spirit, something like chasing the wind. "Under the sun" means in this earthly life. He says he gained no lasting profit from it.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qoheleth), who presents himself as a king in Jerusalem. Tradition holds that it is Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He had tried riches, pleasures and great works, and now he reflects honestly on what truly fills the heart.

For today: enjoy your work and your achievements as a gift from God, but do not expect them to give you ultimate meaning. Put your life first in God, and everything else will find its place.
exp.4:5:
It says we should not let our words lead us into sin. The phrase about making your flesh sin is rendered as the mouth bringing us into guilt. "The angel" most likely refers to the messenger of the temple, though some understand it as an angel of God; there is no complete certainty. Saying "it was ignorance" means making an excuse after a promise made carelessly. God can become angry and undo what we have worked for.

The author is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though this is debated. He is teaching how to approach God with reverence. Just before this, he speaks of promises made to God, which must be kept. Afterward, he warns against many empty words and calls for the fear of God.

For today: before promising something to God or to others, think carefully. Make only promises you can keep, and if you fail, admit it with humility, without excuses.
exp.6:16:
It says not to live in wickedness, not even "much," and that one should not act with foolishness. A "fool" is someone who does not think or weigh the consequences. The closing question warns that such a life can be cut short: "before your time" means before what would be normal.

The Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate this, speaks here. He has just said that life is confusing: sometimes the righteous suffer and the wicked live long. That is why he advises against going to extremes. This verse does not permit sinning "a little"; rather, it warns against wickedness and foolishness. Then it is balanced by the fear of God.

For today: do not trust your own shortcuts or impulsive decisions. Before acting, ask yourself whether it is wise and whether it pleases God, and ask him for direction.
exp.11:8:
The Preacher, the verse says, grew wiser, and the wiser he became, the more he devoted himself to teaching the people what he knew. "He gave ear" means that he weighed carefully and paid close attention to what he was saying, and "sought out" means that he examined things with care. He also "set in order" many proverbs, that is, he arranged them or put them into written form. Words like "fue" and "é" are old-fashioned spellings of "was" and "and."

The one speaking is the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth), whom tradition identifies with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. After reflecting on the emptiness of life, the book here begins to draw to a close and presents his work as a teacher, giving weight to his instruction.

For today: if God has given you understanding, do not keep it only for yourself. Share it with humility, after studying it well, to help others live wisely.
exp.8:6:
This verse invites the person to go, eat their bread with joy, and drink their wine with a merry heart. The reason it gives is that God already looks with favor on what that person does. "Go" is like saying "go on" or "move ahead." "Bread" and "wine" stand for the simple things of everyday life.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qoheleth), who reflects on how brief and mysterious life is. Earlier he spoke of how death comes to everyone and there will be no more chance to enjoy what happens under the sun. For that reason he encourages receiving today's good things with gratitude. Scholars debate his tone: some see it as realistic advice, and others as a celebration of God's gifts.

For today: the next time you eat, do it without rushing or anxiety. Give thanks to God, enjoy the company, and receive that simple moment as a gift from him.
exp.7:1:
Here the author advises obeying the king's orders. He says "I counsel you," that is, "I warn you." "Keep" means to carry out with care. "The oath of God's word" refers to the promise made before God, perhaps an oath of loyalty to the king.

The one speaking is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, a teacher who reflects on life. He has just praised the wise person, and now he gives an example of practical wisdom: living well under authority. The verses that follow speak of the power of the king. Some think the oath was a promise of loyalty; others think it reminds the reader that all authority is under God.

For today: keep your commitments and your duties toward those in authority, such as your work and just laws, with respect and honesty. And when you have promised something before God, do not take it lightly.
exp.1:3:
It says that the one speaking undertook great projects: he built important works, he built houses for himself, and he planted vineyards. "I made me great works" means that he made things that were bigger and bigger. "I builded me houses" is "I built me houses," and "I planted me vineyards" is "I planted me vineyards," that is, he made them for himself.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qohelet), who according to tradition is Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He is conducting an experiment: testing pleasures, wealth, and achievements to discover what is truly good for human beings in this life. That is why he lists what he built and planted.

For today: it is good to work, create, and enjoy what God gives, but achievements by themselves do not fill the heart. Before you invest all your energy in a goal, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God and to the people you love.
exp.6:1:
It is better to visit a house where there is mourning than a house where there is feasting, because death is the end of every human being. Mourning is the sorrow over someone who has died; a feast is a banquet. The sentence about the wise person setting their mind to it means they will think carefully and reflect.

The book presents these words as those of the Teacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He seeks what is worthwhile in life "under the sun." Here he uses proverbs to show that sadness and the reality of death can teach us more than constant amusement.

Today we can stop running away from difficult subjects. Accompanying a family in their grief, or setting aside a moment to think about how brief life is, helps us live with more humility, gratitude and wisdom, and to ask God to teach us to number our days well.
exp.10:0:
It says to cast your bread upon the waters, that is, to give or invest what you have, and that after many days you will find it again. "Bread" stands for provision or possessions, and "find" means you will receive a fruit or result.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qohelet, who reflects on life and its uncertainties. Some read the verse as advice on generosity; others read it as advice to take wise risks in seafaring trade. The verses that follow support both ideas: share among several, because we do not know what evil may come. Its point is to act with courage even when we do not control the future.

Today, be generous and steady in doing good, without expecting immediate payment. Help, sow, and share in faith, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.4:8:
It says that the harvest of the land is for everyone. Even the king depends on the fields to live. "Profit" means fruit or benefit, and "subject" means that he depends on them. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and some translate it as the king being served by the field.

The one speaking is the Preacher, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some dispute this. He has just spoken of injustices and of officials who take advantage of one another. This verse reminds us that no one, however powerful, lives without what the land gives. The text then warns about the love of money.

Today: remember that everything you have comes from God's provision, not only from your power or your money. Give thanks for your sustenance and share generously.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that oppression, that is, abuse or unjust pressure, can make even a wise person lose good judgment. It also says that "el presente," which here means a bribe or gift given to bend a decision, harms the heart and corrupts it.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who reflects on life "debajo del sol." He comes from speaking about the rebuke of the wise and the empty laughter of the fool. Some understand that it shows how fragile even the wise person is; others, that it speaks of judges or authorities. The text allows both readings.

Today it reminds us that no one is immune to pressure or to the temptation of money. It is wise to guard the heart, to ask God for self-control, and to surround ourselves with honest people who correct us in time.
exp.7:14:
This verse says the author commends joy. According to him, the best thing a person can have in this life, "under the sun," is to eat, drink, and be merry, and that this gladness should stay with them in their labor during the days God gives them. "Under the sun" means in this world, in the present life.

The author of Ecclesiastes is called "the Preacher" or Qoheleth. Many associate him with Solomon, although this is debated. He has just observed that sometimes the righteous fare as the wicked do, and this seems to him unjust and meaningless. Faced with this mystery, he does not recommend living without restraint, but receiving God's simple gifts with thankfulness.

For today: do not wait to understand everything before giving thanks. Today, enjoy a meal, your work, or the company of your family as a gift from God, and trust Him with what you do not understand.
exp.9:0:
Dead flies, the verse says, are enough to spoil the finest perfume and make it give off a bad smell. In the same way, a little foolishness can ruin a person who has a reputation for wisdom and honor.

The book is attributed to the Preacher, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He reflects on life and contrasts wisdom with folly. This verse opens a theme that continues in the verses that follow: the fool gives himself away by his own actions and words.

A single rash decision, a burst of anger, or a lie can damage years of good reputation. Today we can take care of the small details: what we say on social media, and how we treat others when we think no one is watching. And when we fail, let us ask forgiveness from God and from the people we have hurt.
exp.3:7:
He describes a man who lives alone, with no child or brother, and yet works without stopping. His eyes are never satisfied with seeing his money, but he never asks for whom he works or why he denies himself the enjoyment of life. "Vanity" means something empty and fleeting that does not fill. "Sore travail" is a heavy and painful task.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qohelet, whom many traditionally identify with Solomon, although this is debated. He observes life "under the sun" and shows how empty it is to work only to gain more. This example prepares his praise of companionship, which comes next.

For today: check why you work. Set limits on your work, and keep time for rest, for your family and friends, and to share what you have. People are worth more than profits.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that the person to whom God gives the ability to enjoy their work and their possessions does not dwell on how brief or burdensome life is. Some translations express this idea as God keeping them occupied with the joy of their heart.

The speaker is the Preacher (Ecclesiastes), traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. After reflecting on the emptiness of riches and striving, he concludes that enjoying with gratitude what one has and one's work is a gift from God, not something that is earned or controlled.

For today: practice gratitude in simple things, such as a meal, your work, or time with your family. Instead of living anxious about the past or the future, receive each day as a gift from God and thank him from the heart.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that the fool talks and talks without stopping. What is striking is that, even so, no one knows what will happen tomorrow, and no one can tell us what will happen after we are gone. "Multiplying words" means talking too much. A "fool" is someone who acts without wisdom and without fear of God.

The book attributes itself to the Preacher, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. Here it contrasts the words of the wise, which bless, with those of the fool, which begin badly and end in nonsense. The fool speaks as if he controlled the future, but the future is not in his hands.

For today: before giving an opinion or promising something with great certainty, pause. Speak less, listen more, and remember that the future is in God's hands. Say with humility: "God willing."
exp.9:17:
It says that when someone is lazy and neglects their work, the house falls into ruin. If a leak is not fixed in time, the roof sags and the rain gets in.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He is speaking about rulers who are not held accountable. This verse uses a simple image: just as an abandoned house decays, a country or a neglected life also falls apart.

For today: think of a small task you have been putting off, such as a bill, a repair, or an unfinished conversation. Do it this week. Small neglects, attended to in time, prevent big problems.
exp.5:3:
It says that the child born dead (the "stillborn" of the verse before) came "in vain," that is, leaving no trace. It goes "into darkness," meaning into forgetfulness and the darkness of death, and even its name is covered, with no one remembering it.

The speaker is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on life "under the sun." Here he describes someone with riches and honor who is unable to enjoy them. With a harsh comparison, he says that such an empty life is worse than that of one who never saw the light. Interpreters debate whether he is speaking of the child or of the rich man; the general sense is dissatisfaction.

For today: do not measure your life only by what you achieve or accumulate. Learn to give thanks and enjoy with simplicity what God gives you, and seek what endures, such as faith and love.
exp.3:14:
He says that the writer looked at all the people of this world, "all the living who walk under the sun," and saw that they all followed the young man who came up to take the throne in place of the earlier king. The "second child who will stand up in his stead" is the young man who takes the king's place. "Under the sun" means in this earthly life.

The Preacher, or Qohelet, reflects on life. He comes from telling that a poor but wise young man is better than an old and foolish king. But here he notes that fame lasts little: the people cheer for one, and then for another. Scholars debate whom the account refers to, and this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: do not place your hope in the applause of people or in passing success. Seek to please God and to live with wisdom and humility, for only what we do for Him endures.
exp.0:7:
It says that everything in life is full of weariness and effort, so much that no one can fully describe it. No matter how much we see, we never feel satisfied with seeing; no matter how much we hear, the ear is never filled with hearing. The words "is not satisfied" and "filled" carry the sense of the verse's own wording, as the text is rendered above.

It speaks of "the Preacher" (Qohelet), which is traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. It comes after speaking of the wind and the rivers, which move on without stopping. With these images it shows that life under the sun seems to be a repeated cycle that never truly satisfies.

Today we can recognize that seeing more, hearing more, or having more does not fill the heart. Instead of running after the next novelty, let us rest in God, and receive with gratitude the simple things of each day.
exp.6:19:
It says that across the whole earth there is no one who is completely righteous, who always does good and never goes wrong. Everyone, even those who try to live well, fails at some point. The word "just" here means someone upright before God and before others.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. Earlier he advises fearing God and seeking wisdom; then he warns not to be troubled by what others say, since you yourself have also spoken badly about people. This verse brings us back down to earth: no one is perfect, not even the wise.

For today: when someone criticizes you or lets you down, remember that you also fail. This helps you respond with humility and patience, and to forgive, while still seeking God sincerely.
exp.9:14:
It says that the work of the fool wears him out, because he does not even know the way to the city. The word for "fool" here refers to someone who does not listen to wisdom and does not think carefully about what he does.

The book is attributed to the Preacher (Qohélet), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some people dispute this. Here it contrasts the wise person with the fool. Just before, it speaks of the fool's many empty words, and then it moves on to criticize irresponsible rulers. The verse shows that foolishness is noticed both in speech and in work.

For today: before you exert yourself, ask questions, make a plan, and seek advice. Hard work serves you better when you know where you are going, and asking for direction from God and from wise people prevents useless weariness.
exp.8:17:
This verse says that wisdom is worth more than weapons of war, meaning that thinking clearly and acting with good judgment can accomplish more than force. But it also warns that a single person who does wrong, the "sinner," can ruin many good things. "Destroyeth" here means to spoil or do harm.

The speaker is the Preacher, the teacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate its author. Shortly before, he tells the story of a small city saved by a poor wise man whom no one remembered. Through this he shows that wisdom is powerful but fragile: the world often ignores it, and one serious mistake can undo a great deal.

For today: value wise counsel before acting in haste or in anger. And take care with your decisions, because one bad act, such as a lie or a deception, can harm your family, your work, or your church.
exp.1:24:
The verse is a question that does not expect an answer: who enjoyed food and well-being more than I did? Here the word "can eat" speaks of enjoying food, and "hasten hereunto" refers to giving oneself pleasure, enjoying life. Some scholars point out that the original text is difficult in this phrase, and that other translations read something different, such as "without him," that is, without God, who can enjoy?

The speaker is the Preacher, traditionally identified with Solomon, a man with more than enough riches and pleasures. After seeking happiness in everything, he concludes that true joy is not achieved by work and accumulation alone, but is a gift that comes from the hand of God.

For today: receive the everyday with gratitude, such as a meal, your work, or rest, as a gift from God, and not as the reward of your effort.
exp.10:1:
He says we should give to several people, "seven, and also eight," that is, generously and more than seems necessary. The reason is that no one knows what misfortune may come upon the earth.

The book is written by "the Preacher" (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. It speaks of the uncertainty of life. Since we cannot control the future, it advises acting with generosity and not being paralyzed by fear. The previous verse speaks of casting bread upon the waters, an image of giving with confidence.

For today: do not hold everything back out of fear of what might happen. Set aside a part of your time or your money to help several people in need. That way, if difficult days come, you will have sown kindness, and perhaps others will help you in return.
exp.2:9:
It says the author has observed the task or burden that God has placed on human beings for them to occupy themselves with. "Labor" here can mean toil, effort or striving, and the phrase "for them to be occupied in it" means that God allowed us to have something to strive over.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He has just spoken of the seasons of life, and he asks what profit there is in so much effort. He will later say that God made everything beautiful in its time, but that we cannot grasp the whole of his work.

For today: accept your work and your occupations as part of the life God gave you, without weighing them down with the anxiety of understanding everything. Do well what falls to you, give thanks for what you have, and trust that God sees the whole picture.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that when a person dies, the body returns to the dust of the earth, from which it was formed, and the spirit returns to God, who gave it. The word "shall return" in the verse above corresponds to the idea of "turning back" to the earth, and the word "gave" is the same as the verse's "gave it." There is a difference between what happens to the body and what happens to the spirit.

The one speaking is the Preacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just described old age and death in poetic images. He speaks above all to young people, encouraging them to remember their Creator before the hard days come (12:1). How to understand the "spirit" here is interpreted in different ways.

For today: our life is brief and belongs to God. It is worth living today with gratitude, reverence and purpose, without putting off our relationship with Him.
exp.6:27:
Here the Preacher says that he keeps searching for something he has not found. Among a thousand men he found one who was truly upright, but among all the women he found none. "A thousand" is a figure of speech meaning that uprightness is extremely rare.

The one speaking is Qohelet, the Preacher, a wise man who examines life by looking at things closely, one at a time. His complaint is harsh and almost bitter. But the next verse corrects it: the problem is not one particular sex, since God made human beings upright and all of us have gone astray through our many schemes. Some scholars believe he is speaking of his own personal experience.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or look for perfect people. Recognize that all of us stumble, starting with you, and return to the uprightness with which God created us.
exp.9:16:
It says that a country is happy when its ruler comes from a noble family and its leaders eat at the proper time, to regain their strength and not to get drunk. "Blessed" means happy or favored. "Feast" refers to food that gives strength. "Son of nobles" can be understood as someone of worthy lineage or of noble character; scholars interpret it in both ways.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qohelet, who reflects on wisdom and foolishness. This verse contrasts with the previous one, where an immature king and leaders who give themselves to feasting from morning on are lamented. It shows how the self-control of rulers affects an entire people.

For today: whoever has some responsibility, at home, at work, or in the church, needs self-control. Ask God for help to use your schedule, your meals, and your pleasures well, so that you can serve others better.
exp.2:4:
It says there are different seasons for opposite things. "Scattering stones" and "gathering" stones together; "embracing" and "refraining from embracing," that is, showing affection or holding back. About the stones there are several interpretations: some think of clearing or ruining a field, or of building; others see an image of affection and intimacy. It is not known with certainty.

The one speaking is the Teacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He is reflecting on life under the sun. He acknowledges that God governs the seasons and that we do not always understand them.

For today: before you act, ask yourself what this stage calls for. There are times to draw near and comfort, and other times to keep a wise distance. Ask God for discernment so that you do not do the right thing at the wrong moment.
exp.8:16:
This verse says that the quiet words of a wise person are heard and are worth more than the shouting of a ruler among fools. "Quiet" means calm, without noise. "Cry" is a loud shout. "Ruler" here refers to someone with authority, not to God. "Fools" are people who do not want to think or learn.

The Preacher, the teacher of Ecclesiastes, speaks here, reflecting on life under the sun. He has just told the story of a poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten. Even so, he concludes that wisdom is worth more than strength, even though the world does not always recognize it.

For today: you do not need to raise your voice to be right. Speak with calm, humility, and good judgment, even when others shout or do not give you credit. The peace of your words can go further than the noise.
exp.0:14:
This verse says that there are things in life that are crooked, meaning damaged or unjust, and that no human effort can make them straight. It also says that what is lacking, what is incomplete, cannot be counted, because it does not exist to be added up. The phrase about what is lacking speaks of what is absent or defective.

The Preacher speaks here, and according to tradition he is Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has investigated with wisdom everything that happens under the sun, and he concludes that human effort has limits. He does not say this with bitterness, but with honesty about a world marked by imperfection.

For today: do not carry the idea that you must fix everything. Do with your hands what you really can do, and hand over to God what you cannot change, such as injustices, mistakes from the past, or the failures of others. Recognizing your limits frees you from anguish and draws you closer to trusting Him.
exp.5:7:
It says that, in the end, the wise person seems to have no advantage over the fool, and that the poor person gains nothing by knowing how to get along among the living. This last phrase can be understood in several ways: knowing how to handle life well, or knowing how to survive with the little one has. Either way, the question is rhetorical: what good is all of that if no one is left satisfied?

The Preacher (Ecclesiastes) speaks, examining life "under the sun." He has just said that work is for filling the mouth and yet the desire is never satisfied. Everyone ends up in the same place, death. He shows the frustration of seeking fulfillment only in human efforts.

For today: do not place your peace in your achievements, your wisdom, or your financial situation. All of that has value, but it is not enough to fill the soul. Be thankful for what you have today and seek God as your true satisfaction.
exp.5:11:
Nobody can know for certain what is good for a person during this short life. Here "vanity" means something fleeting, like a breath or a vapor. Life passes like a shadow, quickly and without lasting. Also, no one can tell us what will happen on this earth after we die.

The book is attributed to the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. It comes after statements that everything is already determined, that we cannot contend with God, and that many words solve nothing. It shows the limits of human wisdom for understanding life on its own.

For today: recognize that you do not control or know the whole future. Instead of living anxiously or seeking final answers in your plans, trust God, live with humility, and gratefully make the most of the day He gives you.
exp.2:6:
It says there are different moments for opposite things. "Tear" can mean ripping a piece of cloth, something done as a sign of grief or mourning; "sew" would be mending it. It also says there is a time to keep quiet and another time to speak. It is a pair of examples of how life changes from one stage to another.

The one speaking is the Teacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. This poem (3:1-8) shows that life has rhythms we do not fully control. Afterward, the author asks what profit there is in so much toil, and that leads him to reflect on trusting God.

For today: before you respond in a discussion, ask yourself whether it is a time to speak or a time to be silent. Sometimes a timely word helps, and other times silence heals. Ask God for wisdom to discern which it is.
exp.1:9:
Here the writer tells us that he did not deny himself anything his eyes wanted to see or have. Nor did he refuse his heart any pleasure. His heart took delight in all his toil, and that joy was the reward he received for so much work. "Toil" means hard labor or effort, and "portion" means reward.

The one speaking is the Preacher, or Teacher (Qohelet), who presents himself as a king in Jerusalem. Tradition links him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He carries out an experiment: testing riches, music, pleasures, and achievements to see whether they give meaning to life. In the next verse he concludes that all of it was vanity, something fleeting that does not fill the heart.

For today: enjoying your work and the good things of life is not wrong, but it is not enough to give us purpose. Ask yourself what you are chasing in order to feel complete, and give God the center of your life.
exp.3:8:
Two people together are better than one, because their work brings them more return. Here it does not speak only of money, but of the benefit gained from working in company.

The book attributes it to the "Preacher," who is traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has just described a man alone, without family, who works without stopping and never asks for whom he is doing it. He calls this "vanity," that is, something empty. Then he shows that companionship gives meaning, help, and comfort when someone falls.

Today we can seek out and value healthy companionship: a family, a church, friends, or colleagues. Let us not do everything alone. Let us ask for help and help others, and so our work and our lives will bear more fruit and more joy.
exp.6:7:
It says that the end of a matter is worth more than its beginning. "Matter" here means any affair or undertaking, not only a business deal. It also says that the person who is patient in spirit, that is, who can endure and wait calmly, is better than the one who is proud in spirit, that is, arrogant and impatient.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), whom tradition has identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. In this chapter he reflects on what is truly good in a short and difficult life. Earlier he spoke of oppression and the empty laughter of the fool. Afterward he warns against hasty anger. Patience ties the whole passage together.

For today: when something starts out hard or slow, such as a job, a relationship, or a prayer that has not been answered, do not rush ahead or get angry. Give God time, and wait for the end with humility and calm.
exp.3:10:
This verse says that if two people sleep together, they give each other warmth, but someone who sleeps alone has no one to keep them warm. The phrase "they have heat" in the verse is simply the idea that two people together stay warm. The verse's wording that they will "keep warm" means they cover and warm each other. It is a simple example of how companionship helps.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on life "under the sun." Earlier he spoke of loneliness and of work that has no meaning for someone with no one to share it with. Here he gives examples of the advantages of having company: better reward for labor, help when someone falls, warmth, and protection. It is usually understood as a general principle about friendship and community, not only about marriage.

Today: do not walk alone through hard times. Seek a friendship or a faith community where you can give support and also receive it.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the author looked again with careful attention and saw all the violence and abuse in the world. He saw the tears of the oppressed, with no one to comfort them, while the power was in the hands of those who mistreated them.

The one speaking is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on life "under the sun," that is, on this world as seen from a human point of view. Tradition links him to Solomon, though some scholars debate this. Here he expresses his grief at injustice, and that is why, in the verses that follow, he reaches a very bitter conclusion.

For today: do not look the other way when others suffer. Be the comforter who is missing, with a visit, a kind word, or concrete help, and carry those who suffer to God in prayer.
exp.8:2:
It says that, among all the things that happen in this life, there is something painful: the same end awaits all of us, death, no matter how we have lived. It also states that the human heart is full of evil and of madness while we live, meaning foolishness and stubbornness. And after that life, a person goes to the dead.

The speaker is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, who in this book observes life from what can be seen in this world. Many believe it is Solomon, though this is debated. He does not deny that God judges, but he points out that, at first sight, death seems to treat the righteous and the wicked alike, and this troubles us.

For today: since life is brief and the heart tends toward error, do not postpone what matters. Ask God for wisdom, correct what you need to correct, and live each day with humility and gratitude.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that light is sweet, and that it is a pleasure for the eyes to see the sun. The word "sweet" here means pleasant, delightful. It speaks of how good it is simply to be alive and to enjoy each day.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qohelet, who reflects on life. He often says that everything is fleeting. Before this verse, he teaches that we cannot control or fully understand everything God does, so it is wise to work with diligence. Afterward, he reminds us that dark days will come and that God will judge. So the joy of this verse is a gift from God, but it is lived with wisdom.

Today you can pause to be thankful for something simple: the morning light, a meal, a conversation. Enjoy it without guilt and without forgetting God, who gives it to you. Live content, but with responsibility.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that when there are many dreams, there are also many empty things and many words. "Vanities" refers to things without worth or fruit that do not last. "Fear God" means to respect him with reverence and to take him seriously. The conclusion is simple: in the midst of so much talking and imagining, you honor God.

The one speaking is the Preacher, as the author of Ecclesiastes presents himself, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some dispute this. He has been speaking about worship and vows, that is, the promises made to God. He warns the reader not to make promises carelessly or to talk too much before him.

For today: before you promise God or other people something, think carefully about whether you will be able to keep it. Talk less, be sincere, and live with respect for God. An honest life is worth more than many fine words.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that whoever removes or moves stones works hard and can be hurt by them, and that whoever splits wood is put in danger by that same labor. The word "moving" here means shifting something from one place to another or changing its position. The phrase "will be endangered" means that the person will face risk.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. In this passage he gathers proverbs about the risks of everyday life. The verses before it speak of falling into the pit one has dug, and the verses after it speak of being wise and not working blindly. He teaches that every task carries its dangers, and that wisdom helps us avoid them.

For today: before beginning a difficult or risky task, think, prepare, and ask God for wisdom. Use the right tools and seek counsel from others. In this way you will work with more care and with less harm.
exp.6:21:
This verse says that your own heart knows well that you too have spoken badly of other people many times. It is an honest reminder that all of us fail with our tongue.

The one speaking is the Preacher, or Qohelet, who reflects on wisdom and the limits of being human. According to tradition, he is associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. It comes from saying that no one is completely righteous. That is why he advises not to take offense at every comment, such as that of a servant who speaks badly of you.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you, before reacting in anger, remember the times you have done the same. This helps you respond with humility, forgive more quickly, and not live preoccupied with what others say.
exp.3:13:
This verse speaks of someone who came out of prison and became king, while another, born into the throne, ended up poor. The word for prison refers to the jail. "Born in his kingdom" may refer to the old king, who fell into misery. Some think the young wise man is the one who comes out of prison, but this is not entirely clear.

The speaker is the Preacher, Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, although not everyone accepts this. He observes that life turns in many directions: a poor but wise youth surpasses a foolish king. But then he adds that people also grow tired of the new leader. He calls all of this "vanity," something fleeting.

Today we can learn that power, fame and success are not secure. Seek wisdom and humility, and place your hope in God, not in the applause of people.
exp.4:16:
This verse describes a person who spends their whole life "eating in darkness," that is, living in sadness, enjoying nothing. It is full of anger, pain and misery. The phrase "in addition to this" is the sense of the words that open the verse. Some understand the darkness as sorrow and bitterness; others take it as living in the dark out of greed, unwilling to spend even on a lamp.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qoheleth, traditionally associated with Solomon, though this is debated. He has just said that a person leaves this world as naked as they came. Working only to accumulate, without enjoying life or trusting in God, is like labor that comes to nothing.

For today: do not live as a slave to anxiety about having more. Give thanks for the bread of today, rest, and enjoy your work and your family as a gift from God, as the verses that follow say.
exp.1:1:
This verse shows that the author looked honestly at laughter and pleasure. To laughter he says it is mad, meaning it deceives or is not as sensible as it seems. Of pleasure he asks what it accomplishes, because he finds in it no lasting benefit.

The speaker is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He conducts an experiment: he tests joy and possessions to see whether they give meaning to life. His conclusion is that, on their own, they are vanity, something fleeting that does not fill the heart.

For today: enjoy what is good without asking it to give what it cannot give. Ask yourself whether what you seek to make you happy leaves you with real peace or only a moment of distraction. Put your heart first in God.
exp.3:12:
It says that a young man without money but wise is better than an old king who is foolish and no longer accepts advice. The word "foolish" means stupid or senseless, and the phrase about not accepting advice means refusing to be corrected or guided. What matters is not age or power, but wisdom and the humility to listen.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. In this chapter he reflects on life under the sun: oppression, loneliness, and the value of companionship. The verse continues the theme that it is better not to be alone or closed off to others. The verses that follow describe a change of power, and their exact interpretation is debated.

For today: seek advice and accept correction, no matter your age or position. Ask wise people, listen with humility, and do not let pride close your ears.
exp.11:3:
It says that, with old age, the body gradually fades. "The doors shall be shut in the streets" may refer to the lips or to a shrinking social life. "The grinding" is the mill: its low sound could stand for eating or for weak speech. "Rise up at the voice of the bird" suggests a light sleep that wakes at the first song. "The daughters of musick" are the songs, or the ability to hear them, which fade away.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), who advises young people to remember their Creator before the hard years arrive. He uses poetic images, and scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of each one.

For today: do not put off your life with God. Today you have strength, hearing and time; use them to pray, serve and love. And if you are already living through years of weakness, remember that God is still sustaining you.
exp.6:15:
It says not to be "righteous over much" or "wise overmuch," because that can lead to ruin. "Destroy thyself" means ruining yourself or harming yourself. It does not speak of being wicked, but of going to extremes.

The Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some dispute this, speaks here. He has just observed that sometimes the righteous perish and the wicked live long. His advice seems to warn against self-righteousness, religious pride, or believing that by behaving perfectly we control what God will give us. It can be interpreted in several ways, but the next verse rejects wickedness and concludes that whoever fears God will come out well.

For today: seek to live with integrity and wisdom, but with humility. Do not use your effort to show off or to demand an account from God; trust in his grace and fear the Lord.
exp.6:20:
It says not to set your heart, that is, your attention and your feelings, on everything people say. If you do, you may hear your servant (your employee or household worker) speaking badly of you.

The quoted words "á" and "aplicar el corazón" are old forms that mean "to" and "giving too much importance to."
