The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, who seeks wisdom for life. He has just said that no one is perfectly righteous. So if we all fall short, it is only natural that others will sometimes speak badly of us too. The next verse confirms this: you too have spoken badly of others.

For today: do not live on alert for every comment, bit of gossip, or criticism. Before you take offense, remember that you too have failed with your words. Listen humbly to whatever is true, let the rest pass, and respond with grace.
exp.1:8:
Here the writer says that he became very great and had more riches and fame than all who ruled before him in Jerusalem. The word "great" means that he rose in position, and "increased" means that his possessions grew. Moreover, his wisdom did not leave him: it stayed with him while he tested all of this.

"The Preacher" of Ecclesiastes speaks, who presents himself as the son of David and king in Jerusalem, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He is conducting an experiment: he looks for whether success, pleasure and possessions give true meaning. Later he concludes that all of that, without God, is vanity.

We can enjoy with gratitude what God gives us, but not base ourselves on achievements or on things to feel complete. Today, give thanks for something you have and ask yourself: what place do I give God in my goals?
exp.1:16:
He says the writer came to hate life. Everything done "under the sun," that is, in this world, weighed on him as heavy and troubling. The verse of "tiresome" as meaning wearying or unpleasant is rendered here as: the work done under the sun was grievous to him. "All is vanity" means something empty and fleeting, like vapor. "Vexation of spirit" is like chasing the wind: much effort that catches nothing.

The Preacher, called Qoheleth, speaks, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just noted that the wise and the fool die alike and both will be forgotten. Moreover, what he built will be left in the hands of someone who may not know how to use it. His bitterness comes from looking at life without considering God.

For today: if you place your worth only in achievements, money, or recognition, sooner or later you will feel emptiness. Entrust your work to God and seek Him first; then what you do has lasting meaning.
exp.8:10:
He says that in life things do not always turn out as one expects. The fastest does not always win the race, the strongest does not always win the battle, and the wise, the prudent, or the one who speaks well does not always obtain bread, riches, or esteem. "I returned" is the way he describes looking again at what he had seen; the swift are those who run quickly; those who speak well are the eloquent.

The one speaking is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, traditionally associated with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He observes life "under the sun," that is, from what can be seen in this world. He does not deny the value of effort; he shows that the outcome is not in our hands, and for that reason he invites us to live with gratitude and to work with enthusiasm.

Today, put effort into doing your work well, but do not place your worth in the results. When something goes wrong, do not condemn yourself; when it goes right, be humble. Entrust your times to God.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that human beings and animals share the same fate: all of them die. "Event" means what happens to someone, their end. "Breath" is the breath of life, and "vanity" means something fleeting, like vapor that vanishes. If we look only at this life, a man does not seem to have any advantage over a beast.

The Preacher is speaking, and in Ecclesiastes he reflects on life as it is seen "under the sun," that is, from an earthly point of view. He has just said that God will judge everyone, and that he allows death so that human beings will recognize their frailty. Some understand that he speaks from a limited human perspective, not as a complete teaching about eternity.

For today: remembering that life is brief helps us live with humility, not to set our hearts on passing things, and to use our time well, trusting in God.
exp.6:14:
The writer says he has seen something that seems unfair: good people who die young even though they live uprightly, and wicked people who live many years. "Vanity" here refers to a short, passing life, like a vapor (in the verse above, "all things" and "days of my vanity" point to this same sense). The phrase "prolongeth his life" means that he lives a long time.

The speaker is the Teacher of Ecclesiastes, called Qohelet, whom many associate with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He is reflecting on the mysteries of life under the sun. He has just said that no one can straighten what God has made crooked, and that in the day of adversity we should consider. He recognizes that not everything can be understood.

For today: when you see injustice or suffering without explanation, do not lose faith. Keep doing good and trust God, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.6:2:
It says that sorrow is better than laughter, because when the face becomes sad and serious, the heart can be made better. The word "sorrow" here is best understood as grief or serious affliction, not as bad temper. "Laughter" refers to light cheerfulness that does not stop to think. To make better means to improve or correct.

The book is attributed to the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. In this passage it compares mourning with feasts. Its point is that facing death and pain teaches us to live wisely, while constant amusement can distract us from what matters.

Today, do not run from difficult moments or cover them with distractions. If you are going through a loss or a mistake, let that pain lead you to pray, to reflect, and to change what God shows you. Also accompany the one who suffers, without rushing them to "be fine."
exp.9:2:
This verse says that the fool, even when he only walks along the street, shows that his wisdom is lacking. Without realizing it, through the way he acts and speaks, he tells everyone that he is a fool. The word "wisdom" in the verse means good judgment or common sense, and it is the thing that fails him.

The speaker is the Preacher, who in Ecclesiastes reflects on life and wisdom. He has been talking about the wise and the fool: a little folly can ruin a good reputation, just as dead flies spoil good perfume. Here he adds that foolishness cannot stay hidden for long. Then he moves on to speak about how to deal with rulers.

For today: before you speak or act, pause and ask God for wisdom. Our character shows in everyday life, and listening with humility helps us not to display so much foolishness.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that the good the author has seen is to enjoy life with simplicity: to eat, to drink, and to take pleasure in the fruit of one's own work during the days God gives us. "Beneath the sun" means in this earthly life. "His portion" means what falls to him, his share in this life.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, traditionally identified with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He has just spoken of the person who works only for wealth and ends up with nothing, living bitterly and worn out. In contrast to that empty life, he proposes another way of living: to receive with gratitude what God gives.

For today: work diligently, but do not let ambition take away your peace. Right now, take a moment to thank God for your food, your rest, or the fruit of your labor, and enjoy it without guilt or anxiety.
exp.11:7:
This verse repeats the phrase with which the book began: "vanity of vanities." The word "vanity" means something passing, like vapor or breath. Saying "vanity of vanities" is the Hebrew way of saying "the most fleeting of all things." The "preacher" is the teacher who gathers the people to instruct them.

The speaker is the Preacher, whom many identify with Solomon, although the book does not give his name and opinions differ. He has just described old age and death with poetic images: chain, bowl, pitcher, wheel. Everything breaks, the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God. That is why he concludes that life without God has no firm foundation.

For today: do not place your hope in what comes to an end, such as money, fame or success. Enjoy the good things God gives you, but seek God first, because only in Him does your life have lasting meaning.
exp.4:11:
What it says: The one who works sleeps peacefully, whether he has eaten little or much. The rich man, by contrast, cannot rest because of his abundance, an old-fashioned word that means plenty or excess of possessions. His riches, instead of giving him peace, take away his sleep.

Context: The speaker is the Preacher, who according to tradition is Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. He observes that money never satisfies the one who loves it. When possessions grow, so do the people who want to enjoy them, and the owner only looks on. That is why he calls it "vanity," something fleeting that does not fill the heart.

For today: Take care of your rest. If worry about earning or keeping more takes away your peace, hand your anxieties over to God, give thanks for what you have, and seek contentment in the honest fruit of your work.
exp.10:9:
It says the young person should let go of the anger, bitterness, or restlessness they carry inside, and keep away from their body whatever harms it. The years of youth are the years of a young life. "Vanity" here does not mean pride, but something fleeting, like a vapor that quickly vanishes.

The speaker is the Preacher, or Qoheleth, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just encouraged the young to enjoy life, but reminds them that God will judge them. So enjoyment is not living without restraint: youth is good, but brief.

For today: do not let resentment steal your best years. Forgive quickly, take care of your body and your decisions, and make the most of each stage of life with gratitude and wisdom, remembering that it passes quickly.
exp.9:4:
This verse says the author has seen something unjust in life: an error that comes from the ruler, that is, from the one who holds authority. The word "as if it were" is a rendering that means "as though it were." And "proceeding" means it comes from above, arising from the one who commands.

The speaker is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has been speaking about foolishness and about how to deal with an angry superior. Now he notes that the errors of rulers have serious consequences, since the following verses show a world turned upside down: fools placed high and capable people placed low.

For today: if you hold some authority, at home, at work, or in the church, remember that your mistakes weigh more heavily on others. Ask for wisdom, listen to counsel, and correct course in time. And if you suffer because of a superior's error, respond with calm and respect.
exp.8:7:
It says that at all times you should wear white clothes and that oil or perfume should never be lacking on your head. The oil was a fragrant oil, and the word for clothes means garments. In that culture, white clothing and oil were signs of celebration, cleanliness and joy.

The Preacher (Qohelet) speaks here, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He has just said that death comes to everyone and that no one knows what lies ahead. So, in the middle of a brief life full of mystery, he advises enjoying with gratitude the simple gifts of God: bread, wine, marriage and work.

For today: do not wait until everything is settled before you rejoice. Today, thank God for something simple, such as a meal with family or a rest, and enjoy it without guilt, caring for your life with gladness and good spirit.
exp.10:4:
It says we cannot understand everything God does. Just as no one knows which way the wind blows, or how the bones of a baby are formed inside its mother, we do not fully understand the work of God, who makes all things.

The author of Ecclesiastes, who presents himself as "the Preacher," is the speaker here. Tradition associates him with Solomon, although some scholars dispute this. Earlier he said there are things we do not control, such as the rain or where a tree falls. Here he concludes that we should not be paralyzed by not knowing the future, but should act with diligence, as the following verses show.

Even if you do not understand everything or can control the outcome, do with effort today what is yours to do. Entrust the rest to God, whose ways are greater than yours.
exp.4:15:
This verse says it is a great evil for a person to leave this world just as they came, with nothing. "As he came" means naked, without riches. Then it asks: what was the value of so much effort if it was like working for the wind, that is, like trying to catch something that cannot be held?

The speaker is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He observes life under the sun and shows the emptiness of living only to accumulate wealth, which can be lost or left to others. For this reason, he soon recommends enjoying with gratitude what God gives.

Today we can work with diligence, but without making money our goal. Let us learn to thank God for what we have, to enjoy what is simple, and to invest our time in what lasts: faith, family, and love for our neighbor.
exp.8:1:
In this life, the same end comes to everyone: death. It comes to the righteous and to the wicked, to the one who worships with sacrifices and to the one who does not, to the one who swears an oath and to the one who fears to swear. The word for what happens to each person is the event or fate that befalls them, and the word for the pure is the one that refers to ritual cleanness.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. He observes life "under the sun," that is, from what can be seen in this world. He does not deny that God judges, but from our limited view, death seems to treat everyone alike. For this reason the book urges us to think with wisdom.

For today: do not live thinking that obeying God will spare you from every hardship. Serve him with humility, trust that he has the last word, and make the most of the time you have with gratitude.
exp.0:13:
He says that the Preacher carefully observed everything people do in this life, "under the sun," that is, in this world, and concluded that all of it is "vanity," something fleeting like a breath, and "vexation of spirit," which can be understood as chasing after the wind or as a burden that wearies the soul.

The one speaking is the Preacher, called Qohelet in Hebrew. He presents himself as a king in Jerusalem; tradition connects him with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. After seeking wisdom, he notices that human effort, without God, cannot produce lasting meaning or fullness.

Today, this invites us not to place all our hope in achievements, money, or recognition, which cannot sustain the soul. You can work with dedication, but place your trust in God, who gives true purpose to what you do.
exp.6:17:
It is good to hold on to this, and also not to let go of that other thing. In other words, it is wise to keep two things together at once, without swinging to either extreme. The one who fears God, that is, who respects him with reverence, will come through both extremes well.

The speaker is the Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars question this. He has just warned against being overly righteous or overly wise, and against wickedness and foolishness. He is probably cautioning against religious pride as well as moral carelessness. He then reminds the reader that no one is perfect.

For today: seek humble balance. Try to live with integrity, but without thinking yourself superior or demanding perfection of yourself. Acknowledge your failures, do not excuse wrongdoing, and trust God with reverence.
exp.9:10:
There is a comparison here: if the charmer does not act in time, his skill does no good. Some translate that the charmer gains nothing; others, that the serpent bites without warning.

The speaker is the Preacher, who in this book reflects on life and wisdom. Tradition links him to Solomon, though some dispute this. Earlier he spoke of the risks of careless work; now he shows that wisdom acts at the right time, and that words without control also wound, as the following verse says.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether what you say helps or hurts. A careless comment can do harm like a bite. Ask God for self-control and speak with truth and kindness.
exp.9:12:
What it says: The fool begins to speak with nonsense, and the longer he goes on, the worse it gets, until it ends in harmful madness. "Foolishness" is a lack of good sense, and "talk" is speaking without restraint. "Madness" means delirium or nonsense, and here it is added that it is "harmful," that is, that it does damage.

Context: The one speaking in the book is the Preacher (Qohelet), who is traditionally associated with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. In this passage he contrasts the words of the wise, which bring grace, with the words of the fool, which ruin him. His intention is to show that talking much without thinking ends badly, because the fool claims to know the future, but no one knows it.

For today: Before you give an opinion, especially in arguments or on social media, pause and ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, useful, and kind. Speaking less and with more care protects your relationships and your witness.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that the full truth about life and about God's works is far beyond our reach. The phrase "that which is far off" refers to what exists or has happened, and "exceeding deep" speaks of what is hidden and hard to understand. The question "who can find it out?" suggests that no one can fully achieve this through their own effort.

The Preacher speaks, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some dispute this. He has just told how he sought wisdom with all his strength, but felt that it kept slipping away from him. He acknowledges the limits of the human mind, and right after this he goes on exploring folly and error.

For today: accept that you will not understand everything. Study, ask questions, and learn with humility, but trust God when something is beyond you. You do not need all the answers to live with faith and to obey him.
exp.4:9:
He who loves silver is never satisfied with silver, and the same applies to one who loves wealth. Here "is never satisfied" means that he is never full; he always wants more. "Abundance" refers to great riches, and "gain nothing" means that he does not obtain any true or lasting benefit. The writer concludes that this is also vanity, that is, something empty and fleeting that does not fill the soul.

The book is attributed to the Preacher (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars debate this. It comes after speaking of injustices and abusive authorities. He observes that wealth does not resolve the longing of the heart. The verses that follow show that more possessions bring more expenses and more worries, and they take away sleep.

For today: ask yourself whether money is a tool or a master in your life. Practice gratitude for what you have, give generously, and seek the peace that comes from trusting God, not from accumulating.
exp.1:25:
God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the person who pleases him. But to the sinner he leaves the task of gathering and piling up riches, and in the end those goods pass to the one who pleases God. The verse uses the word "gather" for reuniting things, and "knowledge" for what is known. Even so, the writer concludes that this too is "vanity," meaning something fleeting, and "vexation of spirit," like chasing the wind.

The Preacher speaks here, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just tested pleasures, labor, and riches, and has found that they do not satisfy on their own. Earlier he said that enjoying food and the fruit of one's work is a gift from God. Here he insists that this joy depends on God, not on effort.

For today: work diligently, but do not place your hope in accumulating. Ask God for wisdom and a grateful heart, and simply enjoy what he gives you today.
exp.1:14:
He said to himself: if death comes equally to the wise and to the fool, why strive so hard to be wise? He concludes that this too is "vanity," meaning something fleeting, that vanishes like vapor and gives no lasting satisfaction. The words "happeneth" and "happens" in the verse both mean the same thing: to take place, to come about.

The Preacher (Ecclesiastes), whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this, has just said that wisdom is better than folly, but he runs into a painful reality: death comes to everyone. He is testing everything "under the sun," without looking beyond this life.

For today: do not place your worth or your hope solely in your achievements, studies, or intelligence. All of that is good, but it does not save you from death. Seek God first, who gives eternal meaning to what we do.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that if you see the poor being oppressed and their right and justice denied in your region, do not be surprised. "Abuses" are mistreatments, "extortion" is taking something by force or deceit, and the "region" is the area where one lives. The reason given is that one official watches over another official, and above them there is one higher still.

The Preacher (Qohelet), traditionally associated with Solomon, though some dispute this, speaks here. He observes life "under the sun" and sees that bureaucracy and corruption are common. Some understand the "higher one" to be God, who sees everything; others understand it to be only the chain of human authorities. Both readings are possible.

For today: do not grow used to injustice, and do not sink into cynicism. Trust that God sees, and act with honesty and compassion wherever you have influence.
exp.8:9:
It says that we should do whatever is within our reach with eagerness and with all our strength. The reason is that in the grave, meaning the tomb or the place of the dead, there is no longer any work, nor planning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom to act on.

The author of Ecclesiastes, who calls himself the Preacher, is traditionally linked with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He reflects on how brief and uncertain life is on this earth. Earlier he invites us to enjoy what God gives; here he reminds us that no one controls his own time.

For today: do not put off the good you can do right now. Work, love, and serve wholeheartedly and with gratitude, knowing that your days are a limited gift.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that life has distinct and ordered moments: there is a time to be born and another time to die, a time to plant and another time to pluck up what has been planted.

The word "time" in the verse above means an opportune moment or season.

The one speaking is the Preacher of Ecclesiastes, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, although some scholars debate this. He reflects on life under the sun, that is, human experience in this world. This poem shows that we do not control every season; there is an order beyond us that points toward God.

Today we can learn to accept the stages of life with humility, both the joyful and the difficult. When something ends, it does not mean that God has abandoned us. Ask Him for wisdom to recognize what to do now: wait, let go, or begin again.
exp.4:1:
What it says: The verse asks us not to speak in haste or say things carelessly when we stand before God. "Be not rash with thy mouth" makes the point that we should not hurry, and "to utter" means to say or pronounce. The reason is that God is in heaven and we are on earth, that is, He is very great and we are small. Therefore, let our words be few.

Context: The author of Ecclesiastes speaks here, the one called "the Preacher" (Qohelet), whom tradition identifies with Solomon, although some scholars question this. Before this, he speaks of going to the house of God with reverence, and afterward he warns against promises made without thought. He wants worship to be sincere and not merely ritual.

For today: Before you pray or promise something to God, pause. Listen first, think about what you will say, and speak with sincerity and respect, without empty phrases.
exp.6:24:
He says the writer set his whole heart and mind to know, examine, and seek out wisdom and the reason of things. He also wanted to understand the wickedness of folly, that is, of living without good judgment, and the madness of error.

The Preacher, whom tradition identifies with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this, speaks here. He has just acknowledged that, although he tested everything with wisdom, wisdom moved away from him, and what is deep cannot be reached. Even so, he keeps searching honestly, seeking to understand life under the sun.

For today: seek wisdom with effort and humility, but accept that you will not understand everything. Ask God for direction, and let Him guide what your mind cannot grasp.
exp.6:12:
This verse says we should look at what God does and recognize that no one can fix what he has left crooked. The word "straighten" is about making something bent or crooked straight again, and "crooked" describes what God allowed or arranged in a way that is hard to change.

The Preacher speaks here, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He has just praised wisdom and now reflects on the limits of human life. The verses that follow speak of enjoying the good day and considering the day of adversity, because we do not control everything that happens. Some situations in life have no clear explanation.

Today, this invites us to stop struggling against what we cannot change, such as a loss or a limitation. We can ask for wisdom to tell apart what we can improve, and trust God with the rest, giving thanks for the good days.
exp.3:3:
He says that the Preacher noticed something sad: much of people's effort and good work comes from envy. That is, the wording about excellence in work refers to doing things with skill and success, and that stirs jealousy in one's neighbor, that is, the person living next door or the coworker. Vanity means something fleeting and empty, and vexation of spirit is like chasing the wind, which wears a person out and leaves nothing behind.

The Preacher, called Qoheleth, speaks in this book, examining life as it is lived under the sun, without looking beyond it. Earlier he described the oppressions and tears of this world. Now he sees that even work done well can be driven by rivalry. Many believe he is Solomon, although some scholars dispute this.

For today: before you strive to outdo others, ask yourself why you work. Give thanks for the achievements of others, and work to serve God and others, not to compete.
exp.8:14:
It says that in that small city there was a poor man, but a wise one. With his wisdom he managed to save the city from the king's attack. However, afterward no one remembered him.

The phrase "was found in it" means "was in it" in the verse, and the word for "delivered" means "rescued" or "saved."

The Teacher speaks, the one who wrote Ecclesiastes, traditionally identified with Solomon, though some scholars dispute this. He observes life "under the sun" and offers this case as an example: wisdom is worth a great deal, but the world does not always recognize it or give thanks for it. That is why, in the following verse, he concludes that wisdom is better than strength.

For today: do good and act wisely even when no one thanks you for it. And notice the ordinary people who help quietly, so that you can thank them and recognize their worth.
exp.7:3:
This verse says that the word of a king carries authority and power, and that no one dares to call him to account with the question, "What are you doing?" The Hebrew sense of the key word here is rule or authority to command, meaning the power a ruler holds to give orders.

The one speaking is the Preacher (Qoheleth), who watches life under the sun with a wise and realistic eye. Here he advises caution before a ruler: obey, do not act in haste, and do not persist in wrongdoing. Some believe that, by contrast, this also shows that God is the supreme King; others read it only as practical advice about life at court. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: respect those in authority with humility and prudence, without rushing ahead or being stubborn. And remember that all human authority has limits, because in the end we will give account to God.
exp.8:3:
It says that as long as a person is still alive, there is still hope for them. It uses a popular saying: a living dog, though considered worthless, is better than a dead lion, which was regarded as noble and strong. The words "that one" and "among the living" are rendered here as what the verse itself says: among those who are still alive.

The Preacher speaks, reflecting on life "under the sun," that is, from what can be seen in this world. He has just noted that death comes alike to the righteous and the wicked. That is why he stresses the value of being alive: the dead can no longer act or change anything on this earth. Some read it as a sober comfort, others as a lament.

For today: as long as you have life, you have the opportunity to be reconciled, to change, to serve, and to seek God. Do not leave for later what you can do today with love and hope.

sum.7: The writer praises wisdom and advises respecting the king and the commands of God. He acknowledges that no one controls the day of their death, and that sometimes the righteous suffer as if they were wicked, which seems to him to be vanity. Even so, he believes that things will go well for those who fear God, and he recommends enjoying one's work with gratitude, because a person cannot grasp all the works of God.
sum.2: Ecclesiastes 3 says that everything has its season: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time of war and a time of peace. God made everything beautiful in its time, but we cannot grasp the whole of his work. The author sees injustice and death, which makes us equal to the animals, and concludes that the best thing is to enjoy the fruit of our labor with gratitude.
sum.9: Ecclesiastes 10 shows that a little foolishness can ruin a good reputation, and that a fool gives himself away through his actions and his many words. It also teaches that wisdom, prudence, and diligent work are worth more than laziness, and that rulers should be accountable. It ends by advising care in how one speaks about those in authority and about the rich.
sum.10: Ecclesiastes 11 encourages us to be generous and to work boldly, even though we cannot know what will happen, because only God knows and controls everything. It also invites us to enjoy youth and life with joy, remembering that God will judge, and to put away anger and evil, since youth passes quickly.
sum.3: The Preacher sees the oppression, the envy, and the meaningless toil of the person who lives alone and is never content, and he concludes that all of it is vanity. He teaches that it is better to work with a companion, because two people help each other, keep each other warm, and can withstand more. He also shows that fame and power pass away, and people soon forget them.
sum.8: Solomon observes that everyone, both righteous and wicked, ends up the same way in death, and that no one controls their own time. So he invites people to enjoy life with gratitude: to eat bread, to love, and to work while there is still opportunity. He also teaches that wisdom is worth more than strength, although sometimes the poor wise person is forgotten.
sum.0: The Preacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, says that everything is meaningless: nature goes around and around without end, and there is truly nothing new under the sun. He tells how he set out to understand everything through wisdom, but found it was a burdensome task and a grief of the spirit. He concludes that much wisdom brings much trouble and pain.
sum.5: Solomon describes a common evil: a person to whom God gives wealth and honor, yet who cannot enjoy them, while others end up enjoying them. Even if such a person lives many years, if he never enjoys what is good, his life is empty. He concludes that unsatisfied desire and many words are vanity, and that no one knows what is best in this fleeting life.
sum.4: Ecclesiastes 5 teaches us to approach God with reverence, listening more and speaking less, and to keep the promises we make to him. It also warns that loving money never brings satisfaction, and that wealth can be lost. Enjoying your work and what you have, with thankfulness, is a gift from God.
sum.6: In Ecclesiastes 7, the Teacher teaches that wisdom grows when we face sorrow, listen to correction, have patience, and avoid extremes. He admits that no one is perfectly righteous and that he does not understand everything. He concludes that God made human beings upright, but people have gone looking for many schemes of their own.
sum.11: Ecclesiastes 12 invites people to remember God while they are young, before old age arrives, which is described with poetic images, and before the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God. The Preacher says that wisdom guides like goads and firmly fixed nails. The conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments, because God will judge every work.
sum.1: In Ecclesiastes 2, the Preacher tests pleasure, laughter, wine, great works, and riches, and concludes that everything is vanity and yields no lasting gain. He sees that wisdom is better than foolishness, but both die and are forgotten. In the end he says that enjoying one's work is a gift from the hand of God.
